INTRODUCTION

What this book does and how it works

This book has one purpose: to help you use grammar accurately, naturally and confidently when you speak English.

It is not enough to know a rule. The goal is to turn that knowledge into active speaking skill — to choose the right structure, in the right moment, and say it without thinking about it.

Every lesson follows the same path: you speak first, you learn one clear rule, you see how similar structures differ, you practise, and then you speak again — this time with the new grammar in your voice. Each lesson ends with a short review and a self-check, so you always know what you can already do.

The course works for both Intermediate and Advanced learners in the same room. Everyone studies the same core lesson. The core work builds accuracy; the Advanced Upgrade boxes build flexibility, precision and naturalness. Advanced work rewards appropriate, precise use — never complexity for its own sake.

By the end of the course, you should be able to:

• construct grammatically accurate sentences while speaking;

• choose appropriate tenses and sentence structures for your meaning;

• ask questions and respond with greater precision;

• explain experiences, opinions and hypothetical situations;

• connect ideas into coherent spoken responses;

• use a wider range of structures naturally;

• recognise and correct your recurring grammatical mistakes;

• apply learned structures in unfamiliar speaking situations.

Completion of the sixteen lessons is not proof of these outcomes by itself. The Diagnostic Test and the Final Assessment use comparable tasks so that your progress can be seen honestly — and so you know exactly what to work on next.

HOW TO USE THIS BOOK

For students and teachers

For students

Work through the lessons in order: each one builds on earlier material. Always begin with the Speaking Hook — say your answers out loud before you read the rule. The rule then gives you the tool you were already reaching for.

Do the exercises out loud whenever possible. Grammar becomes speech through the mouth, not only through the eyes. Use the Pair Speaking and Real Talk sections as they are designed: no reading from notes.

After every lesson, cover the page and try the retrieval questions. Tick the self-check honestly. Return to the Formula Book (Appendix 1) whenever you review.

Two pathways, one classroom

Pathway

Focus

What to do

Intermediate — Build Accuracy

guided construction, error correction, short clear responses

complete all core practice; use the Intermediate box in each Advanced Upgrade

Advanced — Build Flexibility

choice between structures, subtle meaning, extended arguments

add the Advanced Upgrade work; in speaking tasks, qualify, counter and connect

Both groups can respond to the same topic at different levels: give a clear opinion with two reasons (Intermediate), or qualify your position, address a counterargument and connect ideas with varied structures (Advanced).

For teachers

Keep grammar explanation short and give learners substantial time to produce spoken English. The suggested pacing below is a guide — adjust it to your class length.

Review earlier structures in the review tests and in retrieval practice. Evaluate speaking with the success criteria and the rubric in the Final Assessment — not with rigid model answers. Accept alternative answers where an exercise allows them.

DIAGNOSTIC TEST

Find your starting point — 25 questions · no time limit

Do this test before Lesson 1. Do not study first: the point is to see what you can already do. Mark your score out of 25, then keep the paper — you will compare it with your Final Assessment later.

Part A — Tenses and time (10 questions)

1. I __________ (see) that film last week.

2. She __________ (work) here since 2021.

3. While I __________ (cook), the phone rang.

4. He told me he __________ already __________ (leave).

5. Water __________ (boil) at 100°C.

6. They __________ (build) a new bridge when we visited.

7. I __________ my keys — I can't get in. (lose)

8. Last summer we __________ (go) to Herat.

9. How many books __________ you __________ (read) this month?

10. When I arrived, the train __________ already __________ (leave).

Part B — Structures (10 questions)

11. If it __________ (rain), we'll stay home.

12. I wish I __________ (know) the answer.

13. My phone needs __________. (repair)

14. The report __________ (write) by the team last week.

15. He suggested __________ early. (leave)

16. Could you tell me where __________ ? (the station / be)

17. The girl __________ helped me was very kind. (who / whose / which)

18. I'd rather you __________ (not, smoke) here.

19. Ali is __________ than his brother. (intelligent)

20. Not until midnight __________. (she / finish)

Part C — Use and communication (5 questions)

21. I __________ find my passport anywhere. (mustn't / can't)

22. __________ being very tired, he finished the race. (Despite / Although)

23. She asked me, "Where do you live?" → She asked me __________.

24. It __________ rain later — take an umbrella. (certainty: 50%)

25. I __________ my hair cut yesterday.

Diagnostic answer key

A. 1 saw · 2 has worked · 3 was cooking · 4 had left · 5 boils · 6 were building · 7 have lost / 've lost · 8 went · 9 have … read · 10 had already left

B. 11 rains · 12 knew · 13 repairing (or: to be repaired) · 14 was written · 15 leaving · 16 the station is · 17 who · 18 didn't smoke · 19 more intelligent · 20 did she finish

C. 21 can't · 22 Despite · 23 where I lived · 24 might · 25 had

Score guide: 21–25 — strong base, keep the Advanced Upgrade in sight. 15–20 — solid core; work carefully through both pathways. Below 15 — do the core practice twice and speak every answer aloud; accuracy first, speed later.

LESSON 1 · TENSES FOR REAL COMMUNICATION

Part 1 — Build Strong Sentences | Speaking goal: talk about habits, experiences and changes accurately

Tenses are not a chart to memorise — they are choices you make every time you speak.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Discuss with a partner:

• What do you usually do on a normal weekday? (present simple)

• What are you doing these days to improve your English? (present continuous)

• What did you do last weekend? (past simple)

• What has changed in your life since last year? (present perfect)

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Present simple: facts, habits and routines

Formula

Subject + base verb (+ s/es for he/she/it)

Use it for: habits · facts · fixed timetables · states

Use the present simple when something is generally true or repeated.

Examples

I work in a clinic.

She studies every evening.

The course starts at eight. (fixed timetable)

Remember

Add -s/-es with he/she/it: he works, she studies, it rains.

Rule 2 — Present continuous: happening around now

Formula

Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing

Use it for: happening now · current projects · temporary situations · changing trends

Use the present continuous for what is true around this period of your life.

Examples

I'm working on my pronunciation this month.

More students are learning English online every year. (a change)

Remember

Stative verbs usually stay simple: know, believe, own, seem. → 'I know the answer' (not 'I am knowing').

Rule 3 — Past simple vs present perfect

Formula

Past simple: verb-ed / irregular → a finished time

Subject + have/has + past participle → connected to now

Use the past simple when the time is finished (yesterday, last year, in 2020, when I was a child).

Use the present perfect when the time is unfinished (today, this week, recently, since 2021, for ten years) or when the exact time does not matter — the experience or the result matters.

Examples

I visited Bamyan last summer. (finished)

I have visited Bamyan twice. (experience — no finished time)

She has lived here since 2021. (still true)

Remember

Never put a finished-time word with the present perfect: not 'I have seen him yesterday' → 'I saw him yesterday'.

Rule 4 — Talking about changes and the future

Formula

going to + base verb → plans and intentions

will + base verb → instant decisions, predictions, promises

present continuous + time word → fixed arrangements

For the near future, choose by meaning: a plan you have decided (going to), a decision you make while speaking (will), or an arrangement (present continuous).

Examples

I'm going to take the TOEFL next year. (plan)

That looks heavy — I'll help you. (decision now)

We're meeting the teacher on Thursday. (arrangement)

Remember

In 'if' and 'when' clauses about the future, use the present simple: 'If it rains, we'll stay home.'

Part 3 · See the Difference

Present perfect vs past simple — the choice is about TIME

Past simple (finished time)

Present perfect (now link)

The difference

I lost my keys yesterday.

I've lost my keys.

The left sentence tells when; the right one is about now (I still don't have them).

She worked there for five years. (she doesn't now)

She has worked there for five years. (she still does)

Past simple = finished period. Present perfect = continuing to now.

When did you arrive?

Have you arrived yet?

Past simple asks for a finished time; present perfect asks about the present result.

State verbs vs action verbs

A state verb describes a condition, not an action: know, understand, believe, belong, own, seem, prefer.

These usually take simple forms: 'I understand the rule' — not 'I am understanding the rule'.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. I __________ (see) that film last week.

2. Nadia __________ (work) at the hospital since 2022.

3. We __________ (meet) the new teacher tomorrow at ten. (arrangement)

4. He __________ never __________ (be) to London.

5. Look! It __________ (snow)!

6. My brother __________ (believe) in hard work.

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Correct the mistake: 'I have finished my homework last night.'

2. Correct the mistake: 'She is knowing the answer.'

3. Choose: I (have seen / saw) him yesterday.

4. Choose: How long (do you know / have you known) Sara?

5. Rewrite with going to: 'I intend to study medicine.'

6. Answer naturally: What have you done today so far?

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

Interview your partner. Listen carefully and ask one follow-up question each time.

• What do you usually do at the weekend?

• What are you doing these days that is new?

• What did you do last night?

• What has changed in your life since last year?

Success criteria

✓ uses present simple for habits

✓ uses present continuous for current situations

✓ uses past simple and present perfect with correct time words

✓ asks one natural follow-up question

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill the time words: yesterday / ago / in 2020 → past simple; since / for / recently / this week → present perfect.

• Make three true sentences about yourself: one habit, one current project, one recent experience.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use the present perfect continuous for the activity itself: 'I've been revising all morning.' (and I'm tired)

• Use past simple + present perfect in one sentence: 'I failed twice, but I've learned from both failures.'

• Use 'It's the first time I've…' and 'This is the most … I've ever …' for emphasis.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Speak for one minute: how has your English improved? Name one specific past event, explain what you learned from it, and say what you are still working on now.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ past simple for the specific event

✓ present perfect for the change up to now

✓ present continuous for what is happening these days

✓ clear time expressions (last year, since…, this month)

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Present simple = facts and habits. Present continuous = around now.

• Past simple = finished time. Present perfect = connected to now.

• going to = plan; will = decision now or prediction; present continuous = arrangement.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Say your last weekend in five past-simple sentences.

• Say three things that have changed in your life since 2020.

Watch out

• 'I have seen him yesterday' → 'I saw him yesterday.'

• 'I am knowing' → 'I know.'

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can talk about a habit, a current project and a past experience in one answer.

☐ I chose past simple vs present perfect correctly in the practice.

Quick answers

A. saw has worked are meeting has / been is snowing believes

B. I finished my homework last night. She knows the answer. saw have you known I'm going to study medicine. answers vary

LESSON 2 · TELLING STORIES AND DESCRIBING EXPERIENCES

Part 1 — Build Strong Sentences | Speaking goal: tell a story with background, sequence and clear focus

Good stories have a shape: background first, main events in order, one moment of focus.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Tell your partner a short story (30 seconds): something funny, surprising or important that happened to you.

Now listen to your partner's story. Which moment felt most important? What made it clear?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Past continuous: the background of a story

Formula

Subject + was/were + verb-ing

Use it for: the background · what was happening when something started

The past continuous paints the scene. The past simple puts the events into it.

Examples

I was walking home when I met an old friend.

The sun was setting and the streets were getting quiet.

Remember

'when' usually takes the past simple; 'while' usually takes the past continuous: 'While I was cooking, the lights went out.'

Rule 2 — Past perfect: the earlier past

Formula

Subject + had + past participle

Use it for: the first of two past actions · background that happened before the story

When you tell a story, the past perfect takes the reader one step further back.

Examples

By the time we arrived, the film had already started.

She looked upset because she had lost her wallet.

Remember

After 'by the time', use past simple for the second action: 'By the time the taxi came, we had packed everything.'

Rule 3 — Sequencing a story clearly

Formula

First … Then … After that … Suddenly … Finally …

Earlier that day … · By the time … · As soon as …

Sequence words are the signposts of a story. Without them, listeners get lost.

Examples

First, we waited at the gate. Then, suddenly, the announcement came.

As soon as I opened the letter, I understood everything.

Remember

'as soon as' = the second action happens immediately after the first.

Part 3 · See the Difference

Past simple vs past continuous vs past perfect

Past simple — the events

Past continuous — the scene

Past perfect — the earlier past

What each does

I cooked dinner.

I was cooking dinner when she called.

I had cooked dinner before she arrived.

Simple = the event. Continuous = the scene. Perfect = the earlier action.

He took a taxi.

He was taking a taxi when it broke down.

He had taken a taxi before the rain started.

Each form places the action at a different level of the story.

Story shape: background → event → reflection

Strong stories do three things: set the scene (past continuous), report what happened (past simple), and look back (past perfect or present perfect): 'It was raining… I slipped… I had never been so embarrassed… I've been careful ever since.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. While I __________ (study), the power went off.

2. We __________ (already / eat) when they arrived.

3. First, I __________ (call) the office. Then I __________ (take) a bus.

4. She __________ (walk) along the river when she __________ (see) the smoke.

5. By 2019, he __________ (finish) his degree.

6. The children __________ (play) outside while their mother __________ (rest).

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Combine with while: I read the report. The printer broke.

2. Combine with by the time: We reached the station. The train had left. (use past perfect)

3. Correct: 'When I arrived, he already left.'

4. Add sequence words: tell a three-sentence story about missing a bus.

5. Choose: The phone rang (while / when) I was having a bath.

6. Rewrite as a story scene: 'It rained. I forgot my umbrella. I got wet.' (use past continuous + past simple)

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

Tell a two-minute story from your life. Your partner listens, then asks two follow-up questions.

• Choose: a journey you remember · a day everything went wrong · an important decision you made quickly.

• Include one background scene (past continuous), one earlier action (past perfect), and one final reflection.

Success criteria

✓ background scene is clear

✓ events follow a logical order with sequence words

✓ past perfect marks the earlier action

✓ ending explains why the moment mattered

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill the three levels: background (was/were + -ing), events (past simple), earlier past (had + participle).

• Tell a 30-second story using exactly one 'while', one 'when' and one 'by the time'.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use 'would' for repeated past habits in a story: 'On summer evenings, we would sit outside and talk.'

• Use 'had been doing' for earlier background activity: 'She had been waiting for an hour when the bus finally came.'

• End a story with a present reflection: 'It taught me a lesson I've never forgotten.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Tell a two-minute story: a memorable day in your life. Plan it for ten seconds only — do not write anything. Tell it again to a second partner, better.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ background + main events + ending (clear story shape)

✓ sequence words (first, then, suddenly, finally)

✓ past continuous and past perfect used accurately

✓ the listener can repeat the story's main events in order

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Past continuous = the scene; past simple = the events; past perfect = the earlier past.

• Sequence words make a story easy to follow.

• A good story ends with why it mattered.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Tell a story with exactly one 'while' and one 'by the time'.

• What is the three-part shape of a strong story?

Watch out

• 'When I arrived, he left.' (wrong order) → 'When I arrived, he had left.'

• 'While I was walking, I had seen…' → 'While I was walking, I saw…'

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ My story has a clear background, order and ending.

☐ I used past perfect for the earlier action.

Quick answers

A. was studying had already eaten called / took was walking / saw had finished were playing / was resting

B. While I was reading the report, the printer broke. By the time we reached the station, the train had left. When I arrived, he had already left. answers vary while It was raining and I forgot my umbrella, so I got wet. (answers vary)

LESSON 3 · QUESTIONS, AUXILIARY VERBS, AND FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS

Part 2 — Express Ideas Clearly | Speaking goal: ask clear questions and keep a conversation alive

A conversation is a game of questions. The person who asks well controls the talk — politely.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

With a partner, find out: their favourite way to relax, something they are learning now, and one plan for the future.

Rule for this round: after every answer, ask ONE follow-up question before you speak about yourself.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Forming questions

Formula

Yes/No question: Auxiliary + subject + verb …?

Wh- question: Wh- word + auxiliary + subject + verb …?

Auxiliaries: be · have · do · will · can · should · would …

Every English question needs an auxiliary verb before the subject — except when the question word IS the subject.

Examples

Do you live here? · Are you ready? · Have you finished?

Where do you live? · What happened? (What = subject — no auxiliary inversion)

Who called you? (Who = subject)

Remember

With 'do/does/did', use the base verb after it: 'Did she call?' (not 'Did she called?')

Rule 2 — Direct and indirect (polite) questions

Formula

Direct: Where is the bank?

Indirect: Could you tell me where the bank is?

Embedded order: question word + subject + verb (no inversion!)

Indirect questions use statement word order. They sound polite and professional.

Examples

Do you know how much this costs?

I'd like to know when the results will be announced.

Could you tell me why the schedule changed?

Remember

'Do you know where is the bank?' is wrong. → 'Do you know where the bank is?'

Rule 3 — Follow-up questions: the engine of conversation

Formula

Really? · What happened next? · How about you? · What do you mean?

Why was that? · How did that feel? · What are you going to do about it?

Follow-up questions show you listened. They are the difference between an interview and a conversation.

Examples

A: I changed my job last month. B: Wow — how is it going so far?

A: I failed the first time. B: That's hard. What will you do differently?

Remember

Ask about the CONTENT of the answer, not only the topic. Content follow-ups sound genuine: 'You said it was difficult — what part was hardest?'

Part 3 · See the Difference

Direct vs indirect questions

Direct

Indirect (polite)

Why

Where did you buy it?

Could you tell me where you bought it?

Indirect = polite; notice the statement word order after 'where'.

What time does it open?

Do you know what time it opens?

After 'do you know', the tense can stay, but the word order changes.

Why are you late?

Would you mind telling me why you're late?

Soft openings turn a sharp question into a polite one.

Question word is subject vs object

'Who broke the window?' (Who = subject → no 'did'). Compare: 'Who did you call?' (you = subject).

This is a very common error at every level.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. __________ you ever __________ (try) Afghan pilau?

2. What __________ (happen) at the meeting yesterday?

3. Do you know where __________ ? (the library / be)

4. Could you tell me how much this __________ ? (cost)

5. Who __________ (write) this report?

6. Who __________ you __________ (write) to yesterday?

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Make the question polite: 'Where did you park?'

2. Make the question polite: 'When will the results be ready?'

3. Correct: 'Do you know where is the bank?'

4. Add two follow-ups: 'I'm planning to change careers.'

5. Correct: 'Did she called you?'

6. Write one question with 'How long…' about English study.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

Three-minute interview. Partner A asks; Partner B answers — but every answer must end with a follow-up question back to A. Then swap.

• Choose 3 topics: learning English · a proud moment · a difficult decision · future plans.

• Use at least one indirect question and three follow-up questions per person.

Success criteria

✓ question word order is correct (direct and indirect)

✓ follow-ups react to the content of the answers

✓ the conversation flows — no long silences

✓ each person speaks about the same amount

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill the two orders: 'Where did you go?' vs 'Do you know where you went?'

• Learn five soft openers: Could you tell me… · Do you happen to know… · Would you mind telling me… · I was wondering… · Do you have any idea…

Advanced — build flexibility

• Negative questions show surprise: 'Haven't we met before?' · 'Didn't you get my message?'

• Echo questions show interest: 'You did WHAT?' · 'She said it how?'

• Question tags keep a conversation shared: 'It's getting late, isn't it?' · 'You've met her, haven't you?'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Two-minute conversation challenge: your partner will say only one sentence to start (for example: 'I almost missed my flight last week.'). Keep the conversation alive for two full minutes using only questions and short reactions.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ asks real follow-up questions (about content, not only topic)

✓ uses at least one indirect question

✓ correct question word order

✓ the conversation never stops

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Questions need an auxiliary before the subject — except when the question word is the subject.

• Indirect questions use statement word order: 'Do you know where the bank is?'

• Follow-up questions keep conversations alive.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Ask one direct and one indirect question about the same thing.

• Say three follow-up questions you could use with any partner.

Watch out

• 'Do you know where is the bank?' → 'Do you know where the bank is?'

• 'Did she called?' → 'Did she call?'

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can form polite questions with correct word order.

☐ I can keep a conversation going with follow-ups.

Quick answers

A. have / tried happened the library is costs wrote did / write

B. Could you tell me where you parked? Do you know when the results will be ready? Do you know where the bank is? answers vary Did she call you? answers vary

LESSON 4 · MODAL VERBS FOR REAL-LIFE SITUATIONS

Part 2 — Express Ideas Clearly | Speaking goal: express ability, advice, obligation, permission, possibility and certainty at the right strength

Modals are the volume knobs of English: they control how strong or soft your message is.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Give advice to a friend who says: 'My English is not improving.' Use at least two modals (should, could, might…).

A student asks you: 'Can I leave the class early?' Answer politely with a modal.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — The core modals

Formula

Modal + base verb (no -s, no to: he can swim / not he cans or he can to swim)

can / could = ability · may / could = permission · must / have to = obligation

should / ought to = advice · might / could / may = possibility

Choose the modal by meaning and by how strong you want to be.

Examples

I can speak three languages. (ability)

You should rest. (advice — soft)

You must submit the form by Friday. (strong obligation)

It might rain later. (possibility)

Remember

'have to' is often about external rules; 'must' about the speaker's own strong belief: 'I have to wear a uniform' (the rules say so) · 'You must see this film!' (I strongly recommend it).

Rule 2 — Degrees of certainty

Formula

must be / must have been = almost certainly (positive deduction)

might / could / may be = possible

can't be / couldn't have been = almost certainly not

When you guess based on evidence, the modal shows how sure you are. For the past: must have + participle / might have + participle / can't have + participle.

Examples

She's not answering. She must be in a meeting.

He might have missed the bus.

He can't be at home — his car is gone.

Remember

mustn't = prohibition ('You mustn't tell anyone'); can't = deduction ('He can't be 40!'). These are completely different.

Rule 3 — Politeness in real life

Formula

Would you mind + -ing …? · Could I possibly …? · Would it be all right if I …?

I was wondering if I could … (very polite)

In professional and formal situations, softer modals protect relationships.

Examples

Would you mind closing the window?

Could I possibly move the deadline by one day?

I was wondering if I could ask for your advice.

Remember

'Would you mind + -ing' — the answer 'No' means 'yes, fine': 'Would you mind waiting?' — 'No, not at all.'

Part 3 · See the Difference

must vs have to vs should

must (strong advice)

have to (external rule)

should (gentle advice)

What it shows

You must see a doctor.

You have to see a doctor.

You should see a doctor.

Strong advice from the speaker / external requirement / gentle advice.

He must be tired.

He has to be tired.

—

Deduction (I'm sure) vs requirement (the rules force him).

can't (deduction) vs mustn't (prohibition)

can't = I'm sure it's not

mustn't = forbidden

The difference

He can't be home yet.

He mustn't leave yet.

can't = I'm sure it is not true. mustn't = I forbid it / it is forbidden.

could vs was able to

'Could' describes general ability ('I could swim when I was five'); for one successful past achievement, use 'was able to': 'After an hour, I was able to solve it.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. You look tired. You __________ get some rest. (advice)

2. She __________ speak four languages when she was twelve. (past ability)

3. He __________ be at work — his car is in the car park. (certainty, positive)

4. You __________ touch the wires — it's dangerous! (prohibition)

5. It __________ rain later; take an umbrella. (50% possibility)

6. __________ you mind __________ (open) the window?

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Rewrite politely: 'Open the window.'

2. Rewrite with deduction: 'I'm sure she is at home.'

3. Rewrite with deduction (past): 'Perhaps he missed the train.'

4. Correct: 'He mustn't be at home — his lights are off.' (meaning: I'm sure he is not)

5. Answer naturally: 'Would you mind waiting five minutes?'

6. Give soft advice to someone with a headache (2 sentences with modals).

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

Agree on an answer together. Speak as professionals solving a real problem.

• Scenario: your team must choose ONE: a weekend trip, a new project, a training course. There is a budget and a time limit.

• Use modals to negotiate: suggest (should), offer (could), insist (must), accept possibility (might), refuse softly.

Success criteria

✓ modals show the right strength (advice vs obligation)

✓ polite forms used at least twice (Would you mind… / Could I…)

✓ certainty language used correctly (must be / might be)

✓ a decision is reached and explained

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Sort the modals by strength: must > have to > should > could > might.

• Practise the three deductions: must be / might be / can't be — about people in the room.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use 'must have + participle' for past deduction: 'You must have been exhausted.'

• Use 'would' for polite preference: 'I'd suggest waiting.' · 'Would you prefer tea or coffee?'

• Use hedged obligation for diplomacy: 'We really ought to consider…' · 'It might be worth revisiting…'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Role-play: a client calls with a problem (a delayed order, a bad hotel room, a missed class). One of you is the client (complain with modals); one is the professional (advise, apologise, negotiate with modals). Swap roles after one minute.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ modals match the intended strength

✓ polite professional language

✓ at least one deduction (must be / can't be)

✓ a clear solution is offered

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Modals + base verb. Choose by meaning: ability, advice, obligation, permission, possibility.

• must be / might be / can't be = degrees of certainty; mustn't ≠ can't.

• Softer modals (could, would, might) make requests and advice polite.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Say three deductions about the room (must / might / can't).

• Ask for something very politely using two different soft forms.

Watch out

• 'He mustn't be at home' (I forbid) — if you mean deduction, say 'He can't be at home'.

• 'Would you mind to open…?' → 'Would you mind opening…?'

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I chose the right modal strength in the role-play.

☐ I can give polite advice and deductions with correct forms.

Quick answers

A. should could must mustn't might Would / opening

B. Could you open the window, please? / Would you mind opening the window? She must be at home. He might have missed the train. / He may have missed the train. He can't be at home — his lights are off. No, not at all. (No problem.) answers vary

REVIEW TEST 1

Cumulative review — Lessons 1–4 · 15 questions · suggested time: 20 minutes

Part A — Complete the sentences.

1. I __________ (not/see) him since Monday.

2. While we __________ (wait), the announcement came.

3. Water __________ (freeze) at 0°C.

4. She __________ (study) medicine these days.

5. By the time we arrived, the guests __________ (eat) everything.

6. Look at the sky — it __________ (rain).

7. How long __________ you __________ (know) Nadia?

8. Before the meeting __________ (start), we had already discussed the plan.

Part B — Rewrite, combine or transform.

1. If I __________ (be) you, I would apply for the visa.

2. __________ you mind __________ (close) the door?

3. Do you know where the post office __________ ? (be)

4. Despite __________ (be) very tired, she finished the work.

Part C — Use and communication.

1. Rewrite as a second conditional: 'I don't have time, so I can't help.'

2. Make it polite: 'Where did you park?' (Could you tell me…)

3. Give a deduction: You see a colleague carrying a tennis racket. 'You __________ (be) on your way to a game.'

Answer key

A. 1 haven't seen · 2 were waiting · 3 freezes · 4 is studying · 5 had eaten · 6 is going to rain / will rain · 7 have / known · 8 started

B. 1 were · 2 Would / closing · 3 is · 4 being

C. 1 If I had time, I would help. / If I had more time, I could help. · 2 Could you tell me where you parked? · 3 must be

LESSON 5 · CONDITIONALS FOR DECISIONS AND POSSIBILITIES

Part 3 — Think Beyond the Present | Speaking goal: talk about consequences, alternatives and hypothetical situations accurately

Conditionals are the grammar of thinking ahead — and of imagining other worlds.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Quick answers with a partner:

• What will you do if you pass your exam?

• What would you do if you had one free year?

• What would you have done differently last year if you could?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Zero and first conditional: real situations

Formula

Zero: If + present simple, present simple (facts)

First: If + present simple, will + base verb (real future possibility)

The zero conditional is for facts and automatic results. The first is for real future possibilities and their consequences.

Examples

If you heat ice, it melts. (zero — always true)

If it rains, we'll stay home. (first — real possibility)

Remember

Never use 'will' in the if-clause: 'If it will rain' is wrong.

Rule 2 — Second conditional: unreal or unlikely present

Formula

If + past simple, would + base verb

Use it for: imaginary situations · unlikely futures · advice

The second conditional imagines a different present — or a future that is unlikely.

Examples

If I were you, I'd accept the offer. (advice)

If I had more time, I would learn the piano.

Remember

'If I were you…' (were, not was) is the standard form in advice.

Rule 3 — Third and mixed conditionals: unreal past

Formula

Third: If + past perfect, would have + participle (unreal past)

Mixed: If + past perfect, would + base verb (past cause → present result)

Mixed: If + past simple, would have + participle (present cause → past result)

The third conditional looks back at a past that never happened. Mixed conditionals connect a past cause to a present result (or the reverse).

Examples

If I had left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the flight. (third)

If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now. (mixed)

If I were more careful, I wouldn't have lost my phone. (mixed)

Remember

In speech, native speakers often shorten: 'If I'd known…' · '…we'd have left.'

Rule 4 — Variations worth knowing

Formula

Unless = if not · As long as / provided (that) = only if

Should + subject + verb = very formal first conditional

Were + subject + … = formal second conditional

'Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus.' = 'If you don't hurry…'

'Should you need help, call this number.' (formal)

Examples

You won't pass unless you practise.

I'll come as long as you wait for me.

Remember

'unless' already contains 'not' — don't add another negative.

Part 3 · See the Difference

Second vs third conditional

Second — unreal present

Third — unreal past

The difference

If I had time, I would help you.

If I had had time, I would have helped you.

Now/unreal vs past/unreal. The helping didn't happen in the third.

If I were rich, I would travel.

If I had been rich, I would have travelled.

Imagined present vs imagined past.

Type 3 vs mixed

Third conditional

Mixed (past → present)

The difference

If I had slept earlier, I would have arrived on time. (both past)

If I had slept earlier, I would be fresh now. (past → present)

Mixed conditionals are simply cause and result in different times.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. If you __________ (heat) water to 100°C, it __________ (boil).

2. If it __________ (rain) tomorrow, we __________ (cancel) the trip.

3. If I __________ (be) you, I __________ (apologise).

4. If she __________ (leave) earlier, she __________ (not/miss) the train yesterday.

5. If I __________ (know) his number, I __________ (call) him now.

6. We __________ (go) for a walk as long as the weather __________ (stay) fine.

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Rewrite with unless: 'If you don't register, you can't attend.'

2. Rewrite as a third conditional: 'He didn't study, so he failed.'

3. Rewrite as a mixed conditional (past → present): 'She didn't save money, so she can't buy the car now.'

4. Correct: 'If I will have time, I will help you.'

5. Give advice (2nd conditional): a friend wants to quit their job tomorrow without a plan.

6. Answer naturally: What would you do if you won a large prize?

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

Build one story together, sentence by sentence, using conditionals. Each person adds one sentence and passes the story on.

• Start: 'If I had woken up early this morning…'

• Continue for at least six sentences, mixing 2nd, 3rd and mixed conditionals.

• Then invent a second chain starting 'If the internet stopped working tomorrow…'

Success criteria

✓ conditional forms are accurate

✓ at least one third and one mixed conditional appear

✓ the story makes logical sense

✓ both partners contribute equally

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Memorise one living example per type: 'If you heat ice, it melts.' / 'If it rains, we'll cancel.' / 'If I were you, I'd wait.' / 'If I'd known, I'd have come.'

• Drill the short forms in speech: If I'd… · I'd have… · we wouldn't have…

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use inverted conditionals for formal emphasis: 'Had I known…' · 'Were I in your position…' · 'Should you require assistance…'

• Use 'but for + noun' instead of a full if-clause: 'But for your help, I would have failed.'

• Use 'suppose / supposing (that)…' for playful hypotheses: 'Suppose you had to leave tomorrow — what would you take?'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Decision talk (one minute): imagine your organisation has extra money. Choose between three options (training, new equipment, a trip). Explain what will happen if you choose each one — and what you would have done differently last year with this money.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ first conditional for real consequences

✓ second conditional for unlikely options

✓ third or mixed conditional for the past reflection

✓ clear, logical reasoning

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Zero = facts; first = real future; second = unreal present; third = unreal past; mixed = two times.

• 'If I were you…' is the standard advice frame.

• Never use 'will' in the if-clause.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Say one example of each conditional type (5 sentences).

• Turn one past regret into a third conditional sentence.

Watch out

• 'If it will rain…' → 'If it rains…'

• 'unless you don't hurry' → 'unless you hurry'

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can tell an unreal past situation (3rd) and a past→present link (mixed).

☐ My if-clauses never contain 'will'.

Quick answers

A. heat / boils rains / will cancel (or: 'll cancel) were / would apologise had left / wouldn't have missed knew / would call will go / stays

B. Unless you register, you can't attend. If he had studied, he wouldn't have failed. If she had saved money, she could buy the car now. / …would be able to buy… If I have time, I will help you. answers vary answers vary

LESSON 6 · WISHES, REGRETS, AND HYPOTHETICAL SITUATIONS

Part 3 — Think Beyond the Present | Speaking goal: express preferences, dissatisfaction, regrets and imagined alternatives naturally

English has special grammar for the world as you wish it were. This lesson gives it to you.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Complete honestly and tell your partner:

• I wish I had more time for…

• I wish I could…

• I regret not…

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — wish about the present

Formula

wish + past simple → I wish I knew. (but I don't)

wish + could / would + base verb → ability or change

Use the past form for a present situation you want different. The time is now; the grammar steps back one level.

Examples

I wish I spoke French fluently. (I don't)

I wish I were taller. (were is common in formal use)

I wish I could help you. (but I can't)

Remember

wish + would = complaint about someone else's behaviour: 'I wish you would stop interrupting.'

Rule 2 — wish about the past (regret)

Formula

wish + past perfect → I wish I had studied. (but I didn't)

For regrets about the past, use 'had + participle'. This is the grammar of 'if only I had known…'

Examples

I wish I had taken that job.

If only we had left earlier!

Remember

'If only…!' is more emotional than 'I wish…'.

Rule 3 — would rather and it is time

Formula

would rather + base verb → my own preference

would rather + past simple → someone else's action (polite pressure)

It is (high) time + past simple → it should already be happening

It is time + subject + past simple · It is time to + base verb

'I'd rather stay home.' (my choice) · 'I'd rather you stayed home.' (your choice — notice past form).

'It's time we left.' (= we are late leaving).

Examples

I'd rather cook than order food.

I'd rather you didn't smoke here.

It's high time we started the meeting.

Remember

'had better' = strong advice about the near future: 'You'd better hurry.' It is not the past of 'better'.

Rule 4 — prefer, as if / as though

Formula

prefer A to B · would prefer to X rather than Y

as if / as though + past simple (unreal now) or past perfect (unreal past)

'as if' introduces how something seems — often not real: 'He talks as if he knew everything.' (he probably doesn't).

Examples

I prefer tea to coffee.

She looked as if she had seen a ghost.

Remember

If the comparison is real, keep the tense normal: 'It looks as if it is going to rain.' (probably true)

Part 3 · See the Difference

wish + past vs wish + past perfect

wish + past — now

wish + past perfect — then

The difference

I wish I had a car.

I wish I had bought that car.

Present wish vs past regret. The grammar tells you which world you are in.

I wish I knew the answer.

I wish I had known the answer.

Now vs then.

wish + would vs wish + could

wish + could (ability)

wish + would (willingness)

The difference

I wish I could come.

I wish you would come.

could = ability (about me). would = willingness or change (often about you — complaint or request).

it's time: three shapes

'It's time to go.' (general) · 'It's time we went.' (we are late) · 'It's high time he apologised.' (strong: this should already have happened)

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. I wish I __________ (know) her phone number.

2. I wish I __________ (not/say) that yesterday.

3. She acts as if she __________ (own) the place.

4. It's high time we __________ (make) a decision.

5. I'd rather you __________ (not/tell) anyone.

6. If only I __________ (be) more patient!

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Rewrite as a regret (3rd conditional feel): 'I didn't study harder. Now I regret it.' (use wish)

2. Rewrite politely: 'Stop smoking here.' (use would rather)

3. Correct: 'I wish I have more time.'

4. Correct: 'It's time we will go.'

5. Choose: I prefer (reading / to read) novels rather than (watch / watching) films.

6. Describe something unreal with 'as if': your friend arrived late and covered in mud.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

The complaint-and-fix game. One partner describes things they are unhappy about (using wish). The other offers solutions (using should / could / it's time). Swap after two minutes.

• Choose three areas: studies · work · health · free time · family life.

• Each complaint must use wish; each solution must use a modal or 'it's time'.

Success criteria

✓ wish forms are accurate (present vs past)

✓ solutions use should / could / it's time naturally

✓ the conversation sounds genuine, not read

✓ both roles complete their turns

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Sort your own regrets into present-wishes and past-wishes; say each one aloud.

• Drill: I wish I knew… · I wish I had known… · I wish you would… — one of each, about real life.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use 'If only…!' for emotion: 'If only he had listened!'

• Use 'wish + would' to complain diplomatically in professional English: 'We were hoping the report would be ready by Friday.'

• Use 'as though nothing had happened' style narrative: 'She greeted me as though we had argued yesterday.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Speak for one minute: 'My biggest regret — and what it taught me.' Include one wish (past) and one wish (present), then one sentence of advice for a younger learner.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ wish + past perfect for the regret

✓ wish + past simple (or could) for the present

✓ advice given with an appropriate modal

✓ honest, natural delivery

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• wish + past simple = present wish; wish + past perfect = past regret.

• wish + would = complaint or request about someone else.

• would rather + subject + past = preference about someone else; it's time + past = already late.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Say one present wish and one past regret.

• Say a preference about yourself and one about someone else.

Watch out

• 'I wish I have' → 'I wish I had'.

• 'I'd rather you don't' → 'I'd rather you didn't'.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can express a regret and a present wish accurately.

☐ I can use would rather and it's time in real sentences.

Quick answers

A. knew hadn't said owned made didn't tell were

B. I wish I had studied harder. I'd rather you didn't smoke here. / I'd rather you didn't smoke. I wish I had more time. It's time we went. reading / watching answers vary

LESSON 7 · COMPARISONS BEYOND THE BASICS

Part 4 — Compare and Persuade | Speaking goal: compare clearly and support comparisons with reasons

Comparison is the engine of persuasion: every opinion is a hidden comparison.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

With a partner, complete the comparison and give one reason:

• Online learning is better than… because…

• The most useful skill I have learned is… because…

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Comparatives and superlatives

Formula

short adj: -er / -est (big → bigger → the biggest)

long adj: more / the most (more interesting → the most interesting)

irregular: good → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst · far → further → the furthest

Use the comparative for two things; the superlative for three or more.

Examples

This route is shorter than the other one.

This was the most difficult exam I've ever taken.

Remember

Double comparatives are wrong: 'more better' → 'better'. Use 'than', not 'then': 'better than'.

Rule 2 — as … as and patterns of degree

Formula

as + adj + as · not as + adj + as

twice / three times as + adj + as

the + comparative …, the + comparative …

comparative + and + comparative (getting stronger over time)

'as … as' expresses equality; 'the more …, the more …' expresses linked change.

Examples

She's as experienced as her manager.

The more you practise, the more confident you become.

Prices are rising higher and higher.

Remember

'the more … the more …' uses the same comparative structure twice: 'The harder you work, the luckier you get.'

Rule 3 — Comparing with nuance

Formula

far / much / slightly / a little + comparative

by far + superlative · almost as … as · not nearly as … as

compared to / in contrast to + noun

Degree words make comparisons precise — and precision persuades.

Examples

This one is far more reliable.

The results were slightly better than expected.

In contrast to last year, sales have grown.

Remember

When you compare opinions, compare like with like: price with price, quality with quality — then give a reason.

Part 3 · See the Difference

comparative + than vs superlative

Comparative (two)

Superlative (three+)

Why

This book is better than that one.

This book is the best in the series.

Two things vs three or more.

It is more expensive than mine.

It is the most expensive option.

Comparison vs top rank.

subtle patterns

Pattern

Look-alike

The difference

The sooner, the better.

Sooner or later…

Linked change vs 'eventually'.

He is as tall as his father.

He is almost as tall as his father.

Equality vs near equality — small words, big difference.

weak vs strong persuasion

Weak: 'X is better than Y.' Strong: 'X is far more reliable than Y because it has been tested for ten years.' A comparison without a reason is an opinion; with a reason it is an argument.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. This route is __________ (short) than the motorway.

2. It was __________ (bad) experience of my life.

3. The __________ (much) you read, the __________ (fast) you learn.

4. She sings __________ (beautiful) than her sister.

5. This phone is not __________ expensive __________ the other one.

6. He is by far the __________ (talented) player in the team.

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Rewrite with twice as … as: 'The new laptop costs 2× the old one.'

2. Correct: 'She is more taller than me.'

3. Upgrade the sentence with a degree word: 'This method is better than that one.' (use far + reason)

4. Build a 'the more … the more' sentence about learning English.

5. Correct: 'This is better then that.'

6. Compare two cities you know — two sentences, one comparative, one superlative.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

The recommendation game. Each partner prepares a 30-second recommendation (a city, a book, a way to study). Then each defends theirs — comparisons must come with reasons.

• Use at least: one comparative with a degree word, one superlative, one 'as … as' or 'the more … the more'.

• After both presentations, agree together on ONE choice.

Success criteria

✓ comparative and superlative forms are accurate

✓ each comparison has a reason

✓ at least two degree words used (far, slightly, much…)

✓ a joint decision is reached politely

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill the irregulars: good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, far/further/furthest.

• Practise degree words: far / much / slightly / not nearly — with real comparisons from your life.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use 'by far', 'the single most…', 'the least likely to…' for confident evaluation.

• Use concessive comparison: 'Although X is cheaper, Y is far better value in the long run.'

• Use 'compared with / in contrast to' to frame data like an academic: 'Compared with 2020, participation has doubled.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Persuasion talk (one minute): argue for ONE of these — 'The best age to learn a language' / 'The best way to prepare for the TOEFL' / 'The best investment of one hour a day'. Use at least three comparisons.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ accurate comparative and superlative forms

✓ reasons support the comparisons

✓ degree words add precision (far, slightly, by far…)

✓ the conclusion states a clear choice

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Comparative for two; superlative for three or more; 'as … as' for equality.

• 'the + comparative, the + comparative' shows linked change.

• Persuasive comparisons come with reasons and precise degree words.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Say one comparison with 'far', one with 'the more…the more'.

• Rank three things in your life with superlatives and explain why.

Watch out

• 'more better' → 'better'; 'then' → 'than'.

• Don't compare unlike things: price with price, quality with quality.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can compare with precise forms and degree words.

☐ My comparisons are supported by reasons.

Quick answers

A. shorter the worst more / faster more beautifully as / as most talented

B. The new laptop is twice as expensive as the old one. She is taller than me. This method is far better than that one because it saves time. (answers vary) answers vary This is better than that. answers vary

LESSON 8 · LINKING IDEAS AND BUILDING ARGUMENTS

Part 4 — Compare and Persuade | Speaking goal: organise opinions into coherent, well-linked spoken arguments

Grammar connects sentences; linkers connect thoughts. This lesson is about being easy to follow.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Speak for 30 seconds about: 'Why people learn English.' Then listen to your partner. How many different linking words did you each use?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Contrast and concession

Formula

although / even though + subject + verb (full clause)

despite / in spite of + noun or -ing (no subject + verb!)

however / nevertheless / on the other hand (start a new sentence)

'although' joins two clauses; 'despite' joins a noun phrase. Mixing them is the most common error in this area.

Examples

Although it was raining, we went out.

Despite the rain, we went out.

The plan was risky. Nevertheless, we agreed to it.

Remember

'despite of' does not exist. → 'despite' or 'in spite of'.

Rule 2 — Cause, result and purpose

Formula

because / since / as + clause

because of / due to / owing to + noun

therefore / consequently / as a result (result)

so that / in order to + base verb (purpose)

Notice the two families: + clause (because) vs + noun (because of).

Examples

We cancelled because of the storm.

The storm was severe; therefore, we cancelled.

She left early so that she could catch the train.

Remember

'due to' is best with a noun: 'due to the delay'.

Rule 3 — Building an argument you can say out loud

Formula

POINT → REASON → EXAMPLE → LINK to the listener

Opinion: I believe that … · Reason: This is because … · Example: For instance …

Addition: moreover / what is more / another point is that …

A spoken argument needs a skeleton. Use the same shape every time until it becomes automatic.

Examples

I believe online learning is effective. This is because it allows flexible scheduling. For instance, last year I studied at night after work. Moreover, it is often more affordable.

Remember

Spoken arguments are short. Three well-linked points beat eight unlinked ones.

Rule 4 — Ordering and summarising

Formula

Firstly … · Secondly … · Finally …

In short · To sum up · All in all · In conclusion

Signposting tells the listener where you are going — it reduces effort and increases influence.

Examples

To sum up, the advantages clearly outweigh the costs.

All in all, I would recommend the second option.

Remember

End an argument with a summary sentence — listeners remember the end.

Part 3 · See the Difference

although / despite / however

although + clause

despite + noun/-ing

however = new sentence

The rule

Although it was late, we continued.

Despite the late hour, we continued.

It was late; however, we continued.

One idea, three packages: + clause / + noun / separate sentence.

because vs because of

because + clause

because of + noun

Why

Because I was tired, I stopped.

Because of my tiredness, I stopped.

because + clause · because of + noun. A small word changes the whole grammar.

while / whereas / although

'while' and 'whereas' contrast two equal facts: 'I like tea, whereas she prefers coffee.' 'although' concedes one point against another: 'Although I like tea, I ordered coffee.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. __________ the heavy traffic, we arrived on time. (Despite / Although)

2. __________ being very tired, she finished the report. (Despite / Although)

3. He failed the exam; __________, he did not give up. (however / despite)

4. We left early __________ we could avoid the traffic. (so that / because of)

5. The flight was cancelled. __________, all hotels were full. (As a result / Although)

6. I enjoy city life, __________ my wife prefers the countryside. (whereas / despite)

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Combine with although: 'The task was difficult. Everyone finished.'

2. Combine with despite + -ing: 'She was not selected. She applied again.'

3. Correct: 'Despite of the cost, we decided to proceed.'

4. Build an argument skeleton (point → reason → example) for: 'Reading improves speaking.'

5. Correct: 'Although the cost, we bought it.'

6. Add a summary opener to close: give two opinions about technology in education.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

Mini-debate. Choose a position together by arguing against each other — politely — then swap positions and argue the other side.

• Topic: 'Homework should be replaced by daily speaking practice.'

• Each person must use at least: one although/despite, one cause linker, one result linker, and one summary opener.

Success criteria

✓ linkers are accurate (especially despite + noun)

✓ argument has point → reason → example

✓ the other side is answered (counterargument)

✓ the closing summary is clear

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Sort linkers by job: contrast (although, despite, however) · cause (because, due to) · result (therefore, as a result) · addition (moreover).

• Drill the pairs: although + clause / despite + noun — five real situations.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use 'Not only … but also …' with inversion in formal speech: 'Not only did she apologise, but she also offered a refund.'

• Use concessive balance: 'It is true that …; nevertheless, …' · 'Admittedly, …; even so, …'

• Use 'which' to comment on a whole clause: 'She apologised publicly, which changed the whole mood.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Opinion talk (90 seconds): 'What makes a good teacher?' Structure: opinion → two reasons with examples → one concession → summary. Speak without notes.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ point → reason → example structure is visible

✓ contrast and concession used accurately (although / despite)

✓ cause and result linkers present

✓ summary closes the talk clearly

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• although + clause; despite + noun/-ing; however starts a new sentence.

• because + clause; because of + noun; therefore / as a result show consequence.

• Spoken arguments follow: point → reason → example → summary.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Give a 20-second argument using exactly three linkers.

• Say the same contrast idea with although, despite and however.

Watch out

• 'despite of' → 'despite' / 'in spite of'.

• 'Although the cost…' → 'Despite the cost…' or 'Although it was costly…'

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can link ideas with the right linker family.

☐ My argument has a clear skeleton and a summary.

Quick answers

A. Despite Despite (not 'although' — it needs a clause: Although she was very tired) however so that As a result whereas

B. Although the task was difficult, everyone finished. Despite not being selected, she applied again. / Despite the rejection, she applied again. Despite the cost, we decided to proceed. answers vary — must include point, reason, example Despite the cost, we bought it. / Although it was costly, we bought it. answers vary — must open with To sum up / All in all / In conclusion

REVIEW TEST 2

Cumulative review — Lessons 1–8 · 15 questions · suggested time: 20 minutes

Part A — Complete the sentences.

1. If I __________ (know) his number, I would call him now.

2. I wish I __________ (take) that opportunity last year.

3. This method is __________ (effective) than the old one.

4. While I __________ (read), the lights went out.

5. When we arrived, the guests __________ (already / leave).

6. It's high time we __________ (make) a decision.

7. This option is by far the __________ (good) for our budget.

8. Unless you __________ (hurry), you'll miss the bus.

Part B — Rewrite, combine or transform.

1. Combine with despite: 'The exam was hard. Everyone passed.'

2. Rewrite as a second conditional: 'I don't have a car, so I can't drive you.'

3. Give polite advice to a friend who wants to quit their job without a plan. (2 modals)

4. Make it polite: 'Where is the bank?'

Part C — Use and communication.

1. Rewrite as a mixed conditional (past → present): 'She didn't save money, so she can't buy the car now.'

2. Compare with a reason: 'This course is better than that one.' (use far + reason)

3. Correct: 'Despite of the cost, we decided to proceed.'

Answer key

A. 1 knew · 2 had taken · 3 more effective · 4 was reading · 5 had already left · 6 made · 7 best · 8 hurry

B. 1 Despite being hard, everyone passed the exam. / Despite the difficulty, everyone passed. · 2 If I had a car, I would drive you. / If I had a car, I could drive you. · 3 answers vary — advice with should/could/might · 4 Could you tell me where the bank is?

C. 1 If she had saved money, she could buy the car now. / …would be able to buy… · 2 answers vary — far + comparative + reason · 3 Despite the cost, we decided to proceed.

LESSON 9 · PASSIVE VOICE IN NATURAL ENGLISH

Part 5 — Describe and Explain | Speaking goal: choose between active and passive for the right focus

The passive is not a fancy extra — it is how English focuses on what matters.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Look at these two sentences. Which sounds like news, and which sounds like a story?

• Someone stole my bicycle yesterday.

• My bicycle was stolen yesterday.

Tell your partner about something that happened to you — once with the active, once with the passive. Which version focuses on the result?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — How the passive is built

Formula

be + past participle (the tense lives in 'be')

Present: is/are done · Past: was/were done

Future: will be done · Perfect: has/have been done

Modals: can/must/should be done

To make a passive, change the object of an active sentence into the subject, and put the verb into 'be + participle'.

Examples

They clean the office every day. → The office is cleaned every day.

They will announce the results tomorrow. → The results will be announced tomorrow.

Remember

Add the agent with 'by' only when it matters: 'The novel was written by Atiq Rahimi.'

Rule 2 — When to use the passive

Formula

Use the passive when: the result matters more · the doer is unknown, obvious, or general ('people', 'they') · you want objective or formal tone

News, reports, science and professional English use the passive constantly — because they describe events and processes, not people.

Examples

Mistakes were made in the report. (polite — no blame)

The vaccine is being tested in several countries.

The meeting has been postponed until Monday.

Remember

In everyday stories about yourself, the active is usually better: 'I broke my phone' (clearer than 'my phone was broken by me').

Rule 3 — Reporting verbs and passive patterns

Formula

It is said / believed / thought that …

He is said to be / to have been …

have/get something done (see Lesson 10)

These patterns sound objective and educated — very useful in formal speaking.

Examples

It is widely believed that reading improves writing.

She is said to speak five languages.

Remember

'It is said that he left' = 'He is said to have left.' (the leaving is earlier).

Part 3 · See the Difference

active vs passive: what changes?

Active

Passive

Why

Someone attacked the man.

The man was attacked.

The passive hides the attacker — the event and its result take focus.

The committee approved the plan.

The plan was approved.

Formal and objective: the decision matters, not the committee.

get-passive vs be-passive

'get' + participle is more informal and often emotional or unexpected: 'He got fired.' Compare 'He was dismissed.' (formal). 'Get' is common in speech: 'They got married last year.'

false passives

Some verbs look passive but are not: 'The book sold well.' · 'The door opened.' These describe how something happened, not an action done to it.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. The bridge __________ (build) in 2019.

2. The results __________ (announce) tomorrow.

3. This room __________ (clean) every morning.

4. My wallet __________ (steal) on the bus yesterday.

5. A new policy __________ (just / introduce).

6. The letters must __________ (send) before noon.

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Rewrite in the passive: 'Someone has stolen my bicycle.'

2. Rewrite in the active: 'The decision was made by the board.'

3. Rewrite formally: 'People say that he is the best candidate.'

4. Correct: 'The house was builted in 1990.'

5. Correct: 'My phone was stolen by me.' (make it natural)

6. Report the news with a passive: 'They will close the road tomorrow.'

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

The newsroom. Each partner is a reporter. Describe three events from yesterday (local, personal or world news) using the passive. The editor (partner) asks: who did it?

• Events: an accident · a new opening · a rule change · a sports result · something at work or school.

• Use at least two passives and one reporting structure (It is said / It is believed).

Success criteria

✓ passive forms are accurate across tenses

✓ the agent is given only when it matters

✓ tone is objective and report-like

✓ the editor's questions get clear answers

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill passive formation in four tenses: present, past, future, perfect — with objects from your daily life.

• Learn the reporting pair: 'It is said that…' / 'He is said to…' — three real examples.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use the passive with 'get' for informal emotional colour: 'He got promoted after only six months.'

• Use 'It is claimed / alleged / assumed that…' in formal discussion.

• Use passive + participle clauses in writing-style speech: 'Founded in 1971, the school now teaches over a thousand students.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Ninety-second news brief: report three things that happened this week (in your city, your work or your studies). Use the passive for events and one reporting structure. Finish with one comment in the active voice.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ at least three accurate passive structures

✓ objective reporting tone

✓ agent mentioned only when important

✓ clear final comment (active voice)

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Passive = be + past participle; the tense lives in 'be'.

• Use the passive for results, unknown/obvious doers, and objective tone.

• 'It is said that…' = 'He is said to…' — both are formal and natural.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Put three objects from your room into passive sentences (different tenses).

• Say one formal reporting sentence about a person you know.

Watch out

• 'was builted' → 'was built'.

• Don't use the passive for your own story if the active is clearer: 'I lost my keys' is better than 'my keys were lost by me'.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can form the passive in four tenses.

☐ I choose active or passive for the right focus.

Quick answers

A. was built will be announced is cleaned was stolen has just been introduced be sent

B. My bicycle has been stolen. The board made the decision. It is said that he is the best candidate. / He is said to be the best candidate. The house was built in 1990. I lost my phone. / I had my phone stolen. (answers vary) The road will be closed tomorrow.

LESSON 10 · CAUSATIVE STRUCTURES

Part 5 — Describe and Explain | Speaking goal: talk about services, arrangements, influence and responsibility naturally

English has a special grammar for 'I arranged it — someone else did it'. This is it.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Talk with a partner: what do people usually 'have done' in your city?

• haircuts · repairs · cleaning · deliveries · tailoring

Which do you do yourself, and which do you pay others for? Why?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — have/get something done

Formula

have + object + past participle → arrange for someone to do it

get + object + past participle → the same meaning, more informal

Negative/question: I haven't had it done · Did you get it fixed?

Use this when you arrange or pay for a service. The doer is unimportant or obvious (a professional, a shop, a technician).

Examples

I had my car serviced last week.

She's getting her house painted this month.

We need to have the documents translated.

Remember

This structure often appears in stories about problems: 'I had my phone stolen on the bus.' (something happened to my possession — not a service I ordered!)

Rule 2 — make, let, have, get + person + verb

Formula

make + person + base verb → force (no choice)

let + person + base verb → allow (no 'to')

have + person + base verb → instruct/arrange (informal)

get + person + to + base verb → persuade (with 'to'!)

These four verbs control other people's actions — with different levels of force.

Examples

The teacher made us rewrite the essay.

My parents let me travel alone when I was sixteen.

I'll have my assistant call you.

I finally got my brother to help me.

Remember

'get' is the only one with 'to': 'get someone to do something'.

Rule 3 — Talking about services and arrangements

Formula

I need to have my… done · I'm having my… done on Tuesday

How much do you charge to…? · Could you … for me?

I get my… done at… (regular arrangement)

These chunks are the real-life service English: shops, clinics, offices, travel.

Examples

I get my hair cut at the same place every month.

I'm having my laptop repaired — I hope it's ready by Friday.

Remember

For one action by one person that you do yourself or that isn't a service, use the normal active: 'I fixed my laptop' — not 'I had my laptop fixed' (unless you arranged it).

Part 3 · See the Difference

service vs accident

Service I ordered

Accident that happened

Why

I had my car washed.

I had my car damaged in the storm.

Same grammar, different world: one is a service I ordered; the other is something that happened to me.

causative verbs compared

make — force

let — allow

have — instruct

get — persuade

The relationship

She made me apologise.

She let me leave.

She had me rewrite it.

She got me to help her.

force → allow → instruct → persuade. The grammar tells you the relationship.

make vs let in passives

'make' keeps 'to' when it becomes passive: 'I was made to wait an hour.' But 'let' does not: 'They let me go' → 'I was allowed to go' (we usually avoid 'I was let go' except in fixed expressions).

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. I need to have my suit __________ (alter) before the wedding.

2. When did you last get your hair __________ (cut)?

3. The noise made me __________ (lose) my concentration.

4. They let us __________ (use) the kitchen.

5. I'm having my eyes __________ (test) on Thursday.

6. She finally got her son __________ (eat) the vegetables.

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Rewrite with have: 'I paid someone to service my car.'

2. Rewrite with get (persuasion): 'After much discussion, my friend agreed to drive us.'

3. Correct: 'I will get my car to repair tomorrow.'

4. Correct: 'She made me to wait outside.'

5. Describe something you had done recently (service or accident — say which).

6. Ask politely at a shop: you need your phone screen replaced (causative question).

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

The service conversation. Partner A runs a repair shop / salon / clinic; Partner B has problems with their possessions (car, hair, laptop, phone). Negotiate what will be done, when, and for how much — using causatives throughout.

• Partner B: describe at least three things that need doing (need to have… done).

• Partner A: explain what you will do (I'll have… done), what the customer should do, and the price. Use make/let/get at least once.

Success criteria

✓ causative forms are accurate (have/get + object + participle)

✓ service language sounds natural

✓ prices and times are agreed

✓ the conversation includes influence language (make/let/get)

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill the four causatives: make / let / have / get — one true sentence each about people you know.

• Practise the service chunks: 'I need to have my… done.' · 'When can you have it ready?'

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use 'have someone do' for professional delegation: 'I'll have the team look into it.'

• Use experience-causatives in narrative: 'He had us all laughing for an hour.' · 'The film had me thinking for days.'

• Use 'get round to + -ing' and 'end up + -ing': 'I finally got round to having the flat painted.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Story challenge (one minute): 'A day when everything went wrong.' Use at least two causatives (including 'had something done' or 'had something happen to me'), and explain what you made, let or got someone to do afterwards.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ causative structures used accurately

✓ clear distinction between service and accident

✓ story is easy to follow

✓ at least one make/let/get structure

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• have/get + object + participle = arrange a service (or: something happened to me).

• make = force; let = allow; have = instruct; get = persuade (get + to + verb).

• The passive of 'make' keeps 'to': 'I was made to wait.'

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Say three things you would like to have done this month.

• Describe one person who made you do something and one who let you do something.

Watch out

• 'get my car to repair' → 'get my car repaired'.

• 'made me to wait' → 'made me wait'.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can arrange services with have/get causatives.

☐ I can express force, permission, instruction and persuasion correctly.

Quick answers

A. altered cut lose use tested to eat

B. I had my car serviced. I got my friend to drive us. / After much discussion, I got my friend to drive. I will get my car repaired tomorrow. She made me wait outside. answers vary Could you have my phone screen replaced? / How much would it cost to have my screen replaced?

LESSON 11 · GERUNDS AND INFINITIVES

Part 6 — Speak with Greater Precision | Speaking goal: choose the right verb pattern for your meaning

Some verbs want -ing after them; some want 'to'. Getting this right marks you as advanced.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Finish the sentences — then compare with your partner:

• I enjoy… · I hope… · I avoid… · I decided…

Which verbs feel natural with -ing? Which with 'to'? You already know more than you think.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Verbs that take the gerund (-ing)

Formula

enjoy · avoid · consider · finish · keep · mind · miss · practise · suggest · give up · feel like · can't help + verb-ing

These verbs talk about experiences, reactions and activities as things.

Examples

I enjoy reading before bed.

He avoided making eye contact.

Would you mind opening the window?

Remember

'mind' always takes -ing: 'Do you mind waiting?'

Rule 2 — Verbs that take the infinitive (to + verb)

Formula

agree · decide · hope · intend · learn · manage · offer · plan · promise · refuse · seem · tend · want · would like + to + base verb

These verbs look forward — to intentions, decisions and attempts.

Examples

She decided to change careers.

We plan to visit next spring.

He seems to know everyone.

Remember

'would like to…' is polite desire: 'I'd like to ask a question.'

Rule 3 — Verbs that change meaning

Formula

remember / forget / regret / stop / try / go on / mean

+ -ing → the earlier action · + to → the later action (or purpose)

With these verbs, the pattern is not decoration — it changes the meaning.

Examples

I remember locking the door. (I did it; I recall that)

Remember to lock the door. (don't forget — it comes later)

He stopped smoking. (he quit)

He stopped to smoke. (he paused his walk for a cigarette)

I tried restarting the laptop. (a method)

I tried to open the window. (an attempt)

Remember

'I mean to do it' = I intend to. 'Missing the bus means walking' = results in.

Rule 4 — Gerund as subject and after prepositions

Formula

Verb-ing + … = the activity as a subject

Preposition + verb-ing (about doing · instead of going · before leaving · good at speaking)

A gerund can be a subject: 'Swimming keeps me fit.' After any preposition, use -ing.

Examples

Learning a language takes patience.

She left without saying goodbye.

I'm interested in improving my pronunciation.

Remember

'to' is a preposition in some phrases: look forward to · be used to · object to · devote … to · when it comes to. All take -ing: 'I look forward to hearing from you.'

Part 3 · See the Difference

meaning-changing pairs

+ -ing (earlier action)

+ to (later action)

The difference

I stopped eating sugar.

I stopped to eat something.

quit an activity vs pause an activity for another

I remembered to call her.

I remembered calling her.

did it because I recalled (to) vs recalled the action (-ing)

He tried to move the table.

He tried moving the table.

attempt (to) vs experiment/method (-ing)

need + -ing vs need + to

'The car needs washing.' = 'The car needs to be washed.' The gerund here is passive in meaning. Also: 'My hair needs cutting.'

with prepositions: always -ing

Common traps: 'interested in learning' (not 'in learn') · 'good at explaining' · 'instead of complaining' · 'before leaving' · 'after finishing'.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. Would you mind __________ (help) me with this?

2. She avoided __________ (answer) the question.

3. We decided __________ (accept) the offer.

4. I look forward to __________ (hear) from you.

5. He stopped __________ (smoke) last year.

6. She tried __________ (open) the window, but it was stuck. (an attempt)

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Correct: 'I enjoy to read novels.'

2. Correct: 'I look forward to meet you.'

3. Correct: 'She suggested to go early.'

4. Rewrite with need: 'The room must be cleaned.'

5. Choose and explain: I remembered (posting / to post) the letter. (I want to say: I recall doing it)

6. Make a sentence with 'Instead of…' + -ing about study habits.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking
