Work with a partner

The habits interview. Ask each other about routines, plans and preferences — using gerund and infinitive patterns in every question and answer.

• Questions to adapt: What do you enjoy doing at weekends? What have you decided to change this year? What do you avoid doing? What are you looking forward to?

• Each person must use at least four different gerund/infinitive verbs.

Success criteria

✓ patterns are accurate (-ing vs to)

✓ at least one meaning-changing verb used correctly

✓ conversation flows naturally

✓ follow-up questions asked

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Learn in chunks, not lists: 'I enjoy swimming' · 'I decided to leave' — five chunks a day.

• Drill the meaning pairs: stop/remember/try — with real examples from your week.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use complex subjects: 'Finding time to practise is harder than finding motivation.'

• Use 'there is no point in + -ing' · 'it's worth + -ing' · 'it's a waste of time + -ing'.

• Use 'have difficulty (in) + -ing': 'I had difficulty understanding the accent.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Speak for one minute: 'What learning English has taught me about myself.' Use at least three gerunds and two infinitives. End with one decision you have made (to + verb).

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ gerund and infinitive patterns accurate

✓ at least one meaning-changing verb used correctly

✓ sentences are connected, not listed

✓ the final decision is clear

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Some verbs take -ing, some take 'to', some take both with meaning changes.

• After any preposition, use -ing — including 'to' in look forward to, be used to.

• Gerunds work as subjects: 'Practising daily helps.'

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Say two sentences with 'stop' (both meanings) and two with 'try' (both meanings).

• Name five verbs + -ing and five verbs + to from memory.

Watch out

• 'enjoy to read' → 'enjoy reading'.

• 'look forward to meet' → 'look forward to meeting'.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can choose the pattern automatically with common verbs.

☐ I know the meaning-changing pairs.

Quick answers

A. helping answering to accept hearing smoking to open

B. I enjoy reading novels. I look forward to meeting you. She suggested going early. The room needs cleaning. / The room needs to be cleaned. posting answers vary

LESSON 12 · RELATIVE CLAUSES AND CONCISE DESCRIPTIONS

Part 6 — Speak with Greater Precision | Speaking goal: describe people, places and ideas precisely in one sentence

Relative clauses let you build two ideas into one clean sentence — the mark of fluent speech.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Describe without naming: choose someone in the class, a famous person or a place — describe it so your partner can guess. Use 'who', 'which' or 'that' in every sentence.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Defining relative clauses (essential information)

Formula

who (people) · which (things) · that (both) · whose (possession) · where · when

No commas. Without the clause, the sentence changes meaning.

Object pronouns can be omitted: 'The book (that) I read…'

A defining clause tells us WHICH one. It is part of the meaning, so no commas.

Examples

The woman who called you is my manager.

The town where I grew up has changed a lot.

The man whose car was damaged is waiting outside.

Remember

In speech, drop the object 'that/who/which' when it is the object: 'The film we watched…' (not 'The film which we watched it…').

Rule 2 — Non-defining relative clauses (extra information)

Formula

, who … , / , which … , (commas — like a quiet aside)

Never use 'that' here. Never drop the pronoun.

A non-defining clause adds information about something already identified. It is spoken with a small pause.

Examples

My brother, who lives in Dubai, is visiting next week.

The project, which took six months, was finally approved.

Remember

With commas, the clause can comment on the whole sentence: 'She apologised publicly, which changed the mood.'

Rule 3 — Prepositions in relative clauses

Formula

… the clinic to which I go … (formal)

… the clinic which I go to … (normal)

… the clinic I go to … (speech)

In formal English the preposition moves before the pronoun; in speech it stays at the end.

Examples

The colleague with whom I worked has retired. (formal)

The colleague I worked with has retired. (natural)

Remember

For people after prepositions, use 'whom' in formal English: 'the person to whom I spoke.'

Rule 4 — Reduced clauses: the concision tool

Formula

who is / who was + … → (drop 'who is'): 'The man (who is) standing there…'

which was + participle → 'The results (which were) published today…'

Dropping 'who is/which was' makes descriptions tighter — very useful in speech and reports.

Examples

Anyone wishing to attend must register. (= who wishes)

The documents attached to this email… (= which are attached)

Remember

Only drop 'who is/which was' — never drop a full verb: 'The man who called' cannot become 'The man called'.

Part 3 · See the Difference

defining vs non-defining

Defining (no commas)

Non-defining (commas)

Why

My sister who lives in London is a doctor. (I have several sisters)

My sister, who lives in London, is a doctor. (I have one sister)

The commas change how much we learn: identification vs extra detail.

Students who pass the exam receive a certificate.

My cousin, who passed the exam, received a certificate.

No commas when the clause defines which ones.

that vs which vs who

that (speech, things/people)

which (things)

who (people)

The rule

The book that I bought…

The book which I bought…

The man who helped me…

that is common for things and people in speech; which/who after commas; 'that' never after commas.

whose vs of whom

'The student whose essay won the prize…' is natural in speech; 'the student the essay of whom won…' is possible but clumsy. Prefer 'whose'.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. The girl __________ helped me was kind. (who / which / whose)

2. My phone, __________ I bought last year, has already broken. (that / which)

3. This is the café __________ we first met. (where / which)

4. The man __________ car was stolen is the manager. (who / whose)

5. The results __________ were announced today are surprising. (reduced clause: leave a gap or use which)

6. I read the article you recommended. (insert the omitted pronoun — what is it?)

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Combine: 'The teacher is excellent. She taught me last year.' (use who)

2. Combine with commas: 'My friend is a pilot. He travels constantly.' (extra information)

3. Correct: 'My mother, that lives in Kandahar, is visiting.'

4. Correct: 'The book what I read was amazing.'

5. Reduce: 'Students who are interested in the course should apply.'

6. Describe your favourite place using one defining and one non-defining clause.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

The guessing game. Describe a person, place or object from your life using only relative clauses — never name it. Partner guesses, then swaps.

• Each person describes two items, using at least one defining and one non-defining clause.

• After guessing, improve each other's sentences: make them more concise.

Success criteria

✓ relative pronouns chosen correctly (who/which/whose/where)

✓ defining vs non-defining punctuation/meaning respected

✓ descriptions are concise and clear

✓ partner can guess the item

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill the four pronouns: who / which / whose / where — with people and places from your life.

• Practise dropping object pronouns: 'The film we saw…' · 'The course I chose…'

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use 'which' to comment on a whole clause: 'He apologised, which surprised everyone.'

• Use cleft focus with 'what': 'What I need is time.' · 'What surprised me was the result.'

• Use reduced clauses in formal speech: 'Anyone arriving late will be asked to wait.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Describe-and-explain talk (one minute): talk about a person who influenced you. Use two defining clauses, one non-defining clause, and one reduced clause. Do not write anything.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ relative clauses are accurate and natural

✓ at least one non-defining clause with correct meaning

✓ one concise reduced form

✓ the person's influence is explained clearly

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Defining clauses identify (no commas); non-defining clauses add detail (commas).

• Drop object pronouns in speech: 'The book I read…'.

• Reduced clauses ('who is' dropped) make descriptions concise.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Say one defining and one non-defining clause about people near you.

• Describe your city with two relative clauses and one reduced clause.

Watch out

• 'the book what I read' → 'the book (that) I read'.

• 'My mother, that lives…' → 'My mother, who lives…'

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I choose the right pronoun and punctuation automatically.

☐ I can compress descriptions with reduced clauses.

Quick answers

A. who which where whose (that) were / which were — or simply 'announced today' with 'The results announced today…' that (or which)

B. The teacher who taught me last year is excellent. My friend, who is a pilot, travels constantly. My mother, who lives in Kandahar, is visiting. The book (that) I read was amazing. Students interested in the course should apply. answers vary

REVIEW TEST 3

Cumulative review — Lessons 1–12 · 15 questions · suggested time: 20 minutes

Part A — Complete the sentences.

1. The house __________ (build) in the 1960s.

2. I had my watch __________ (repair) last week.

3. She is said __________ (speak) five languages.

4. He avoided __________ (make) the same mistake twice.

5. This is the café __________ we first met.

6. She is the teacher __________ class inspired me. (who / whose)

7. I'd rather you __________ (not/mention) this to anyone.

8. He talks as if he __________ (know) everything.

Part B — Rewrite, combine or transform.

1. Rewrite with need: 'The room must be cleaned.'

2. Rewrite as a deduction (past): 'Perhaps he missed the train.'

3. Reduce: 'Students who are interested in the course should apply.'

4. Make it formal and passive: 'People believe that the economy is improving.'

Part C — Use and communication.

1. Complete: The __________ (much) you practise, the __________ (confident) you become.

2. Correct the indirect question: 'Do you know where is the bank?'

3. Complete the causative: I __________ my hair cut yesterday.

4. Correct: 'I enjoy to read novels.'

Answer key

A. 1 was built · 2 repaired · 3 to speak · 4 making · 5 where · 6 whose · 7 didn't mention · 8 knew

B. 1 The room needs cleaning. / The room needs to be cleaned. · 2 He must have missed the train. · 3 Students interested in the course should apply. · 4 It is believed that the economy is improving. / The economy is believed to be improving.

C. 1 more / more confident · 2 Do you know where the bank is? · 3 had · 4 I enjoy reading novels.

LESSON 13 · REPORTED SPEECH AND REPORTING VERBS

Part 7 — Sound More Natural and Advanced | Speaking goal: report conversations and summarise information accurately and naturally

Half of real speaking is reporting what other people said. This lesson makes that effortless.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Tell your partner: what did a friend or family member say to you this week? Report the words — don't read them. What exactly did they say?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — The backshift: one step back in time

Formula

Direct: 'I am tired.' → She said (that) she was tired.

Present simple → past simple · Present continuous → past continuous

Past simple → past perfect · will → would · can → could · may → might

would / could / should / past perfect → stay the same

When you report, the verbs usually step back one tense. 'That' is optional and often dropped in speech.

Examples

"I work here." → He said he worked there.

"I've finished." → She said she had finished.

"I'll call you." → He said he would call me.

Remember

If the statement is still true, you may keep the original tense: 'She said the earth goes round the sun.'

Rule 2 — Reporting questions and commands

Formula

Yes/No question: ask + if / whether + subject + verb (statement order!)

Wh- question: ask + question word + subject + verb

Command: tell / ask / order + person + to + base verb

Negative command: told me not to + base verb

Reported questions use statement word order — no auxiliary 'do', no question mark.

Examples

"Where do you live?" → She asked me where I lived.

"Are you ready?" → He asked if I was ready.

"Sit down." → She told me to sit down.

"Don't worry." → He told me not to worry.

Remember

'say' has no object: 'He said that…' · 'tell' needs a person: 'He told me that…' (never 'He said me…').

Rule 3 — Reporting verbs: beyond say and tell

Formula

admit · agree · apologise · argue · claim · complain · explain · insist · mention · promise · refuse · remind · suggest · warn

Patterns: verb + that … · verb + to + verb · verb + person + to + verb · verb + -ing

Reporting verbs make summaries compact and precise — exactly what the TOEFL and professional English require.

Examples

He admitted making a mistake. (verb + -ing)

She promised to call back. (verb + to)

The doctor warned me not to travel. (verb + person + to)

He suggested leaving early. (verb + -ing)

Remember

'suggest' takes -ing or 'that': 'She suggested going' / 'She suggested that we go' (not 'suggested me to go').

Rule 4 — Time and place references

Formula

now → then · today → that day · yesterday → the day before

tomorrow → the next day / the following day · last week → the week before

here → there · this → that · ago → before

When you report later, shift the time words too — or the story makes no sense.

Examples

"I'll do it tomorrow." → She said she would do it the next day.

"I saw him yesterday." → He said he had seen him the day before.

Remember

If you report on the same day, you can keep the time words: 'He said he'd do it tomorrow' (said earlier today).

Part 3 · See the Difference

say vs tell (and ask)

say + that

tell + person

ask + person

The pattern

He said that he was busy.

He told me that he was busy.

He asked me if I was busy.

say + that (no person) · tell + person · ask + person + question

reporting with the same tense or backshift

Reported later (backshift)

Still true now (no shift)

The rule

She said she was tired. (reported later)

She said she is tired. (still true now)

Both can be correct: backshift for reporting later; no shift when the fact is still true — or when you report immediately.

command vs request vs advice

order: told me to wait

request: asked me to wait

advice: advised me to wait

insistence: insisted on my waiting

The force

told me to wait

asked me to wait

advised me to wait

insisted on my waiting

The verb carries the force: order → request → advice → insistence.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. "I am working now." → He said he __________ (work) then.

2. "We have finished." → They said they __________ (finish).

3. "Where did you park?" → She asked me where I __________ (park).

4. "Don't touch it!" → He warned me __________ touch it.

5. "I'll help you." → She promised __________ (help) me.

6. "Let's take a break." → He suggested __________ (take) a break.

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Report: 'I never lie.' (He said…)

2. Report a question: 'When will the results be announced?' (They asked…)

3. Correct: 'He said me that he was tired.'

4. Correct: 'She suggested me to go early.'

5. Report with a strong verb: 'No, I didn't break the window.' (He denied…)

6. Report advice your teacher has given you (2 sentences, 2 different reporting verbs).

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

The message game. Partner A reads (or says) three short messages from 'other people' (notes, emails, quotes). Partner B reports them to a third person (the teacher/another pair) using different reporting verbs. Swap.

• Messages to report: a complaint · a promise · a warning · an invitation · a refusal.

• Use at least four different reporting verbs and both question and command reports.

Success criteria

✓ backshift is accurate

✓ question word order correct in reports

✓ at least four reporting verbs used

✓ time references shifted correctly

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill the backshift table out loud with true sentences about your day.

• Learn the verb patterns in chunks: 'admitted -ing' · 'promised to' · 'warned me not to' · 'suggested -ing'.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use continuous reporting verbs for liveliness: 'She kept insisting that she was right.' · 'He went on to explain…'

• Use 'point out / observe / note' in academic reporting: 'The report points out that demand has fallen.'

• Report with judgement-free precision: 'He claimed to have seen nothing, yet witnesses disagreed.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Retell challenge (ninety seconds): report a real conversation you had this week — a discussion, an argument, an interview or a negotiation. Report at least four things people said, using varied reporting verbs. End with your own comment.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ accurate backshift and time references

✓ varied reporting verbs (not only 'said')

✓ questions and commands reported correctly

✓ clear final comment

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Backshift: one tense back; time words shift too.

• say (+ that) vs tell (+ person); reported questions use statement order.

• Reporting verbs (admit, promise, warn, suggest…) carry meaning and grammar patterns.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Report three things someone said to you today.

• Report one question, one command and one promise — all out loud.

Watch out

• 'He said me…' → 'He told me…'.

• 'She suggested me to go' → 'She suggested going' / 'She suggested that I go'.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can report statements, questions and commands accurately.

☐ I use reporting verbs beyond 'say'.

Quick answers

A. was working had finished had parked (or: parked) not to to help taking

B. He said (that) he never lied. / He said (that) he never lies. They asked when the results would be announced. He told me that he was tired. She suggested going early. / She suggested that I go early. He denied breaking the window. answers vary

LESSON 14 · PARTICIPLES AND ADVANCED SENTENCE PATTERNS

Part 7 — Sound More Natural and Advanced | Speaking goal: combine ideas concisely without losing clarity

Participles are how English professionals compress ideas — speed without confusion.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Combine these ideas aloud, any way you like:

• The team was exhausted. They finished the project on time.

• She opened the letter. She found the news she had waited for.

Which version sounds most professional?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Present and past participles as adjectives

Formula

-ing (present participle) → causes the feeling: a boring lecture

-ed (past participle) → feels the effect: bored students

The rule: things are -ing; people (and animals) are usually -ed — because they feel it.

Examples

The film was fascinating. (the film causes interest)

I was fascinated. (I felt it)

tiring work / tired workers · confusing news / confused readers

Remember

Some -ing words describe a person's behaviour instead: 'He is very interesting' (he holds my attention) vs 'He is very interested' (he feels interest).

Rule 2 — Participial clauses: the professional connector

Formula

Verb-ing …, subject + verb → same time / reason

Having + past participle …, subject + verb → earlier action

Past participle …, subject + verb → passive meaning

Used carefully, these replace 'because/after/while + full clause'

Participial clauses open or close a sentence with compressed information. Use them in formal speech and writing.

Examples

Having finished the report, she left the office. (After she had finished…)

Written in 1963, the novel is still popular. (The novel, which was written…)

Walking to the station, I realised my mistake. (While I was walking…)

Remember

The subject must match! 'Walking to the station, the rain started' is wrong — the rain was not walking. → 'Walking to the station, I got soaked.'

Rule 3 — Absolute and fronted patterns for emphasis

Formula

Fronted participle: 'Considering the costs…', 'Given the evidence…', 'Looking at the results…'

With + noun + participle: 'With prices rising, families are worried.'

Having been + participle: 'Having been warned, we prepared carefully.'

These patterns frame a whole clause — they sound composed and formal.

Examples

Given the circumstances, we agreed to wait.

With the deadline approaching, the team worked faster.

All things considered, it was a success.

Remember

'Given' = when you consider; 'considering' = taking into account; 'all things considered' = final judgement phrase.

Rule 4 — Concise combination: fewer words, same meaning

Formula

'She opened the letter and she read it slowly.' → 'Opening the letter, she read it slowly.'

Two actions → one main verb + participle (if the subject is the same).

Concision is not using difficult words; it is removing whole clauses.

Examples

Because he had not slept, he made mistakes. → Not having slept, he made mistakes.

The report, which was published today, contains errors. → The report published today contains errors.

Remember

Do not over-compress speech. One or two participial clauses per answer is plenty.

Part 3 · See the Difference

-ing vs -ed adjectives

-ing (causes the feeling)

-ed (feels it)

Example

an exciting game

excited players

The game causes excitement; the players feel it.

a tiring day

tired students

The day causes tiredness; the students experience it.

participle clause vs full clause

Participle clause (compressed)

Full clause

Why

Having finished, she left.

After she had finished, she left.

Same meaning; the participle version is compressed and formal.

Written in haste, the report had errors.

The report, which was written in haste, had errors.

Compression with a passive participle.

the subject rule

The understood subject of a participle clause must be the subject of the main clause: 'Opening the door, I felt the cold.' (I opened). Never: 'Opening the door, the room was cold.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. The lecture was so __________ (bore) that half the class fell asleep.

2. We were __________ (amaze) by the results.

3. __________ (finish) his speech, he answered questions.

4. __________ (warn) about the traffic, we left early.

5. __________ the prices rising, families are saving more. (with / despite)

6. __________ (walk) into the room, she noticed the broken window.

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Combine with a participle: 'Because she had studied hard, she passed easily.'

2. Combine with a participle: 'The man who was standing at the door waved.'

3. Correct: 'Opening the window, the cold air came in.'

4. Rewrite with 'Given': 'When you consider the costs, the plan is unrealistic.'

5. Correct: 'I am very interesting in history.'

6. Compress one of your own sentences with 'Having + past participle'.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

The formal briefing. Each partner gives a 60-second briefing on a situation (a project, a trip, an event). The briefing must use at least two participle clauses.

• Include: one 'Having + past participle', one opening with 'Given/Considering/With', and one -ed/-ing adjective pair.

• Partner listens and reports the briefing back in one sentence.

Success criteria

✓ participle clauses have correct subjects

✓ forms are accurate (-ing / -ed / having done)

✓ meaning stays clear after compression

✓ listener's report matches the content

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill -ed/-ing pairs about real life: tired/tiring, confused/confusing, interested/interesting — five sentences.

• Practise the subject rule: make two correct participle openings from your week.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use 'There being + noun': 'There being no further questions, the meeting ended.'

• Use 'Not having… / Never having…': 'Never having travelled abroad, he found the airport overwhelming.'

• Use participles in formal closings: 'Considering all the evidence, we recommend…'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Ninety-second formal recommendation: recommend one policy for your workplace or school (more training, a schedule change, a new rule). Open with 'Considering…' or 'Given…', use one 'Having…' clause, and close formally.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ at least two accurate participle clauses

✓ -ed/-ing adjectives used correctly

✓ recommendation is clear and logical

✓ formal, composed tone

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• -ing adjectives cause feelings; -ed adjectives feel them.

• Participle clauses compress because/after/while clauses — subject must match.

• 'Given…', 'Considering…', 'With + noun + participle' frame formal speech.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Open a sentence with 'Having…' about your day.

• Describe today with one -ing and one -ed adjective.

Watch out

• 'Opening the window, the room was cold.' (subject mismatch).

• 'interesting in' → 'interested in'.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can compress two clauses into one formal sentence.

☐ My participle clauses keep the correct subject.

Quick answers

A. boring amazed Having finished Having been warned / Warned With Walking

B. Having studied hard, she passed easily. The man standing at the door waved. Opening the window, I felt the cold air come in. / As I opened the window, the cold air came in. Given the costs, the plan is unrealistic. I am very interested in history. answers vary

LESSON 15 · HEDGING, EMPHASIS, AND NATURAL INVERSION

Part 8 — Speak with Confidence | Speaking goal: control certainty, emphasis and formality like an educated speaker

The difference between good and excellent English is control: how strong, how sure, how formal.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Two speakers say: 'The plan will fail.' / 'The plan may well fail.' Which sounds more educated? Why?

Give the same opinion twice: once very certain, once carefully hedged. How does the effect change?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Hedging: the art of careful claims

Formula

may / might / could + base verb · may well · it is likely that …

seem to / tend to / appear to · generally / broadly / in most cases

it could be argued that … · one possible explanation is …

Hedging makes claims professional and safe. Academic and business English hedge constantly — it signals control, not weakness.

Examples

The results suggest a small improvement.

This policy may well reduce costs in the long run.

It could be argued that the data is incomplete.

Remember

Too many hedges sound vague: 'It might perhaps possibly be…' — one careful hedge per claim is enough.

Rule 2 — Emphasis: clefts and focus

Formula

It is/was + emphasised part + who/that … (cleft)

What I need is … · What surprised me was … (wh-cleft)

do/does/did + base verb (auxiliary emphasis): 'I do believe you.'

Cleft sentences split one idea in two to put the spotlight on one part.

Examples

It was the price that changed my mind. (not the quality)

What I love about this city is its energy.

She did call — I saw the message.

Remember

In speech, stress the focused word: 'It was JOHN who…'.

Rule 3 — Inversion: formal emphasis

Formula

Negative opener + auxiliary + subject + verb:

Never have I seen … · Not only did she …, but she also …

Rarely / Seldom / Little / Nowhere + auxiliary + subject + verb

Only + adverbial + auxiliary + subject + verb: Only then did I understand …

No sooner … than … · Hardly … when … · Under no circumstances …

When a sentence begins with a strong negative or limiting phrase, English reverses the order — like raising your voice politely.

Examples

Never have I been so surprised.

Not only did he apologise, but he also refunded the money.

Only after the meeting did I understand the decision.

Remember

Inversion is punctuation for the ear. Use it once for impact — never in every sentence.

Rule 4 — Choosing the right level of certainty and formality

Formula

certainty scale: will > must > should > may well > might > could > may

formal markers: passive · inversion · clefts · hedging · full forms

Match the strength of your language to your evidence and your audience. Over-claiming damages credibility; careful claims build it.

Examples

Formal: 'Should you require further information, please do not hesitate to contact us.'

Neutral: 'If you need more information, contact us.'

Casual: 'Just call me if you need anything.'

Remember

The most confident speakers hedge the most — because they know the limits of their knowledge.

Part 3 · See the Difference

certainty levels

Certain: will

Likely: may well

Possible: might

The idea

The plan will succeed. (certain)

The plan may well succeed. (likely)

The plan might succeed. (possible)

Same claim, three levels of commitment.

normal order vs inversion

Normal order

Inversion (emphatic)

The effect

I have never seen such a mess.

Never have I seen such a mess.

The inverted version is emphatic and formal — powerful in speeches, heavy in casual chat.

cleft focus changes meaning

Basic sentence

It-cleft

Wh-cleft

The idea

I met the manager yesterday.

It was the manager who I met yesterday.

What I did yesterday was meet the manager.

Each version puts the spotlight in a different place.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. __________ have I heard such a convincing argument. (Never / Ever)

2. Not only __________ (she / pass) the exam, but she also got the highest mark.

3. Only after reading it twice __________ (I / understand) the letter.

4. The data __________ (suggest) that costs are falling. (hedged claim)

5. It was __________ the deadline that forced us to decide. (focus on the reason)

6. This method __________ (tend) to work better with small groups.

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Hedge the claim: 'This policy will reduce costs.'

2. Make a cleft: 'The price changed my mind.' (focus the price)

3. Invert: 'I had rarely felt so confident.'

4. Correct: 'Never I have seen such a mess.'

5. Say the same request at two formality levels: you need more time for a report.

6. Use 'Not only … but also' with inversion about two of your skills.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

The panel discussion. Question: 'What will work look like in ten years?' Each partner gives a one-minute answer using hedging and at least one emphatic structure (cleft or inversion). Then ask each other one hard follow-up question.

• Plan for ten seconds only. In your answer include: one hedge (may well / tend to / it could be argued), one cleft (It is… that / What… is), and one conclusion.

• Answer the follow-up question carefully — hedging is welcome when you are unsure.

Success criteria

✓ claims are hedged appropriately (not over-hedged)

✓ emphasis structures used accurately once or twice

✓ certainty level matches the evidence

✓ answers stay clear and confident

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Drill the certainty scale out loud: will / must / should / may well / might / could — one claim at each level.

• Learn three inversion frames by heart: 'Never have I…' · 'Not only did…' · 'Only then did…'.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Use 'little did he know…' and 'little did I realise…' in storytelling.

• Use litotes (understatement): 'not unlike', 'no small achievement', 'not bad at all'.

• Use formal conditional inversion in writing-style speech: 'Were this proposal accepted…' · 'Had we known…'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Two-minute formal talk: 'One change that would improve education in my country.' Include: a hedged claim, one cleft sentence, one inversion, and a clear closing. Speak with confidence — no notes.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ hedging used for claims, not for every word

✓ at least one cleft and one inversion — accurate

✓ register is consistently formal

✓ closing states the position clearly

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Hedging (may well, tend to, it could be argued) makes claims professional.

• Clefts and do-emphasis spotlight information: 'It was X that…' / 'What I need is…'.

• Inversion follows negative openers: 'Never have I…' — use for impact, sparingly.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Make one claim at three certainty levels.

• Say one cleft and one inversion from memory.

Watch out

• 'Never I have seen' → 'Never have I seen'.

• Over-hedging sounds vague; over-inverting sounds theatrical.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can control how strong my claims sound.

☐ I can emphasise with clefts and inversion — accurately and sparingly.

Quick answers

A. Never did she pass did I understand suggests (or: suggest) the deadline tends

B. This policy may well reduce costs. / This policy is likely to reduce costs. It was the price that changed my mind. Rarely had I felt so confident. Never have I seen such a mess. answers vary answers vary

LESSON 16 · GRAMMAR IN REAL CONVERSATION

Part 8 — Speak with Confidence | Speaking goal: bring all the course grammar together in free, accurate, confident speech

This lesson is not new theory — it is the moment everything you have learned becomes your voice.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start here — talk first

Warm-up round with a partner: speak for thirty seconds on any topic. Your partner listens and names every grammar structure they recognise (tenses, conditionals, passives…). Swap.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

The course grammar: one map

Formula

TIME: tenses · storytelling · reported speech

CHOICE: modals · conditionals · wishes · gerunds/infinitives

SHAPE: questions · linkers · relatives · participles · passive · causative

STYLE: comparisons · hedging · emphasis · inversion

Every lesson in this course belongs to one of these four jobs. When you speak, ask: what job does my next sentence need?

Examples

Tell the story (time) → explain the cause (choice) → describe the people (shape) → give your view (style).

Remember

Accuracy first, then range. A clear sentence in the right tense beats a fancy one in the wrong tense.

The speaking strategy: three steps to confident speech

Formula

1. THINK the meaning → 2. CHOOSE the structure → 3. SAY it whole

If stuck: simplify — and keep going. Repair later: 'What I mean is…'

Fluency is not speed; it is continuity. Keep the message moving and fix problems as you go.

Examples

'If I would have known…' — stop, repair: 'If I had known, I would have come.'

Remember

Self-repair is a strength in speaking tests — it shows control.

Part 3 · See the Difference

recognition vs use

You already recognise most course structures. The final step is producing them under pressure — that is what the challenges below train.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete or correct the sentences.

1. Fix and explain: 'I have seen him yesterday.'

2. Fix and explain: 'If I will have time, I will help.'

3. Fix and explain: 'Despite of the price, we bought it.'

4. Fix and explain: 'He suggested me to wait.'

5. Fix and explain: 'Never I have been so tired.'

6. Fix and explain: 'I look forward to meet you.'

B. Choose, transform or build.

1. Combine (participles): 'Because he had not slept, he made errors.'

2. Report: 'Don't worry,' she said. (2 forms)

3. Compare with nuance: 'This option is better.' (use a degree word + reason)

4. Make it passive and formal: 'Someone has changed the schedule.'

5. Hedge the claim: 'This method is the best.'

6. Ask a polite indirect question about tomorrow's schedule.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Work with a partner

The grammar gym — four rounds. Each round: speak for one minute on the topic, using the target structures. Partner counts the structures used and gives feedback.

• Round 1 — Storytelling: a challenge you overcame. (tenses, participles)

• Round 2 — Advice: a friend must choose between two jobs. (modals, conditionals)

• Round 3 — Report: what your colleagues or classmates have decided. (reported speech, passives)

• Round 4 — Argument: one change that would improve your school or workplace. (linkers, hedging, emphasis)

Success criteria

✓ structures match the round's target

✓ errors are self-corrected during speech

✓ ideas are clear and well-linked

✓ confidence and continuity are maintained

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

Intermediate — build accuracy

• Re-do any lesson exercise that felt hard — out loud, not on paper.

• For each of the four jobs (time / choice / shape / style), write three sentences from your own life.

Advanced — build flexibility

• Stack structures in one sentence: 'Had I known that the report would be delayed, I would have asked for help.'

• Use style deliberately: open a talk with an inversion, hedge your main claim, close with a cleft.

• Practise repair phrases: 'What I mean is…' · 'Let me rephrase that…' · 'Or rather…'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Speak now — without reading

Final speaking challenge (two minutes): 'How I have changed — and what comes next.' Tell a story, explain a decision, and state a goal. Use at least six different structures from the course. This is also your practice for the Final Speaking Assessment.

Partner feedback — listen for

✓ range of structures used accurately

✓ clear story shape with linking

✓ at least one hedged or emphatic structure

✓ confident, continuous delivery with natural self-repair

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Key learning points

• Course grammar does four jobs: time, choice, shape, style.

• Speak in three steps: think meaning → choose structure → say it whole.

• Accuracy first, then range; self-repair shows control.

Retrieval practice — cover the page, then say

• Name all four grammar jobs and one structure for each.

• Tell a one-minute story using three different course structures.

Watch out

• Choosing complexity over accuracy — simple and correct is always better.

• Freezing on errors — repair and continue instead.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can use structures from at least six lessons in free speech.

☐ I can self-repair and keep talking.

Quick answers

A. I saw him yesterday. (finished time) If I have time, I will help. Despite the price, we bought it. / Although it was expensive, we bought it. He suggested waiting. / He suggested that I wait. Never have I been so tired. I look forward to meeting you.

B. Not having slept, he made errors. She told me not to worry. / She reassured me. answers vary — degree word + reason required The schedule has been changed. This method may well be the best. / This method is probably the best. (answers vary) answers vary — indirect word order required

FINAL ASSESSMENT

Part 1: Grammar knowledge · Part 2: Independent speaking task

Part 1 — Grammar knowledge (30 questions · suggested time: 35 minutes)

Section A — Complete the sentences. (12 questions)

1. I __________ (live) here since 2020.

2. When I got home, my family __________ (already / have) dinner.

3. If it __________ (be) sunny tomorrow, we'll go to the lake.

4. I wish I __________ (not/say) that yesterday.

5. The meeting __________ (cancel) yesterday afternoon.

6. You look exhausted — you __________ (must / work) all night. (past deduction)

7. She avoided __________ (make) any promises.

8. The teacher made us __________ (rewrite) the essay.

9. This is the most __________ (challenge) course I've ever taken.

10. __________ (warn) about the storm, the fishermen stayed ashore.

11. He suggested __________ (leave) before the traffic.

12. Not only __________ (she / apologise), but she also offered a refund.

Section B — Rewrite or transform. (10 questions)

13. Report: 'I'll help you tomorrow,' he said.

14. Report: 'Where did you buy it?' (She asked me…)

15. Polite question: 'When does the shop close?'

16. Third conditional: 'He didn't revise, so he failed.'

17. Passive (formal): 'Someone has stolen the documents.'

18. Cleft (focus the manager): 'The manager approved the plan.'

19. Causative: 'I paid someone to fix the roof.'

20. Inversion: 'She had rarely felt so confident.'

21. Combine with although: 'The task was difficult. They finished it.'

22. Combine with a participle: 'Because he had studied hard, he passed easily.'

Section C — Use and communication. (8 questions)

23. Choose: He (mustn't / can't) be at home — his car is gone.

24. Complete with a linker: __________ being expensive, the course is worth it.

25. Hedge the claim: 'This method is the best.' (may well / probably)

26. Compare with nuance: 'Option A is better than Option B.' (use far + give a reason frame)

27. Correct: 'The book what I read was amazing.'

28. Complete: The more you practise, the __________ (confident) you become.

29. Report advice: 'You should apply early,' she said. (She advised…)

30. Complete with the right pattern: I look forward to __________ (meet) you.

Answer key — Final Assessment

A. 1 have lived / 've lived · 2 had already had · 3 is · 4 hadn't said · 5 was cancelled · 6 must have been working · 7 making · 8 rewrite · 9 challenging · 10 Having been warned · 11 leaving · 12 did she apologise

B. 1 He said he would help me the next day. · 2 She asked me where I had bought it. · 3 Could you tell me when the shop closes? · 4 If he had revised, he wouldn't have failed. · 5 The documents have been stolen. · 6 It was the manager who approved the plan. · 7 I had the roof fixed. · 8 Rarely had she felt so confident. · 9 Although the task was difficult, they finished it. · 10 Having studied hard, he passed easily.

C. 1 can't · 2 Despite · 3 This method may well be the best. / This method is probably the best. (answers vary) · 4 Option A is far better than Option B because… (answers vary) · 5 The book (that) I read was amazing. · 6 more confident · 7 She advised me to apply early. · 8 meeting

Accept alternative answers where the exercise allows them (e.g. 'may well' / 'probably' / 'is likely to' for hedging). Compare this score with your Diagnostic Test score — the difference is your progress.

FINAL ASSESSMENT — PART 2

Independent speaking task and evaluation

Speaking task (2 minutes to prepare · 2 minutes to speak)

Speak on ONE of the following topics:

• A decision that changed your life — and what you would do differently today.

• One change that would improve education or work in your country.

• A person who influenced you, and the advice they gave you.

You may make brief notes during the preparation time. Speak without reading a script.

APPENDIX 1 · GRAMMAR FORMULA BOOK

Sixteen cards — one per lesson. Review with this book closed first.

Card 1 — Tenses for Real Communication

Present simple = facts & habits · Present continuous = around now

Past simple = finished time · Present perfect = connected to now

going to = plan · will = decision/prediction · present continuous = arrangement

Card 2 — Telling Stories

Past continuous = the scene · past simple = the events · past perfect = the earlier past

when + past simple · while + past continuous · by the time + past perfect before past simple

Shape: background → events (First… Then…) → ending/reflection

Card 3 — Questions and Follow-ups

Wh- + auxiliary + subject + verb · Yes/No: auxiliary + subject + verb

Indirect: question word + subject + verb (no inversion) — 'Do you know where the bank is?'

Follow-ups keep conversations alive: 'Really? What happened next? How about you?'

Card 4 — Modal Verbs

Modal + base verb: can/could = ability · may/could = permission · must/have to = obligation · should = advice · might = possibility

must be = certainly (positive) · might be = possible · can't be = certainly not

mustn't = prohibition ≠ can't (deduction) · Would you mind + -ing?

Card 5 — Conditionals

Zero: If + present, present · First: If + present, will + verb

Second: If + past, would + verb · Third: If + past perfect, would have + participle

Mixed: If + past perfect, would + verb · unless = if not · no 'will' in if-clauses

Card 6 — Wishes and Regrets

wish + past simple = present wish · wish + past perfect = past regret

wish + would = complaint/request · If only…! = strong emotion

would rather + base (me) / + past (someone else) · It's (high) time + past

Card 7 — Comparisons

comparative + than (two) · the superlative (three+) · as + adj + as

the + comparative, the + comparative · comparative + and + comparative

far / much / slightly / by far + comparison · comparisons persuade with reasons

Card 8 — Linking and Arguments

although + clause · despite / in spite of + noun or -ing · however = new sentence

because + clause · because of + noun · therefore / as a result = consequence

Argument skeleton: POINT → REASON → EXAMPLE → SUMMARY

Card 9 — Passive Voice

be + past participle (tense lives in 'be'): is done · was done · will be done · has been done · must be done

Use: result matters · doer unknown/obvious/general · objective tone

It is said that … = He is said to …

Card 10 — Causative Structures

have/get + object + participle = arrange a service (or: something happened to me)

make + person + base (force) · let + base (allow) · have + base (instruct) · get + to (persuade)

'get' keeps 'to' — the other three don't.

Card 11 — Gerunds and Infinitives

enjoy/avoid/mind/suggest/keep + -ing · decide/hope/plan/promise/refuse + to

remember/forget/stop/try: -ing = earlier action · to = later action

Preposition + -ing — including 'to' in look forward to / be used to

Card 12 — Relative Clauses

who (people) · which (things) · that (both) · whose · where — object pronouns can drop

Defining = no commas (identifies) · Non-defining = commas (extra detail, no 'that')

Reduced: 'the man (who is) standing there' — only drop who is / which was

Card 13 — Reported Speech

Backshift one tense: present → past → past perfect · will → would · can → could

ask + if/whether or question word + statement order · told/asked + person + to

say (+ that) vs tell (+ person) · time words shift: tomorrow → the next day

Card 14 — Participles

-ing adjective = causes feeling · -ed adjective = feels it (boring lecture / bored class)

Participle clause: 'Having finished, she left.' — subject must match the main clause

Frames: Given… / Considering… / With + noun + -ing

Card 15 — Hedging, Emphasis, Inversion

Hedge: may well / might / tend to / it could be argued that …

Cleft: It was X that … / What I need is … · do-emphasis: 'I do believe…'

Inversion after negative openers: Never have I… / Not only did… / Only then did…

Card 16 — Grammar in Real Conversation

Four jobs: TIME (tenses, reported) · CHOICE (modals, conditionals, wishes) · SHAPE (questions, linkers, relatives, passives) · STYLE (comparison, hedging, emphasis)

Think meaning → choose structure → say it whole

Accuracy first, then range; repair and continue: 'What I mean is…'

APPENDIX 2 · COMMON ERRORS AND CORRECTIONS GUIDE

Thirty errors that mark learners — and the fix for each

✗ Error

✓ Correction

Why

I have seen him yesterday.

I saw him yesterday.

finished time needs past simple

I am knowing the answer.

I know the answer.

state verbs take simple forms

She is more taller than me.

She is taller than me.

no double comparatives

This is better then that.

This is better than that.

than (comparison) not then (time)

If it will rain, we'll stay.

If it rains, we'll stay.

no 'will' in if-clauses

If I would have known…

If I had known…

third conditional: if + past perfect

I wish I have more time.

I wish I had more time.

wish + past for unreal present

I'd rather you don't smoke.

I'd rather you didn't smoke.

would rather + subject + past

It's time we will go.

It's time we went.

it's time + past (already late)

Despite of the cost…

Despite the cost… / In spite of the cost…

no 'despite of'

Although the cost, we bought it.

Despite the cost, we bought it.

although + clause; despite + noun

Do you know where is the bank?

Do you know where the bank is?

indirect questions use statement order

Did she called you?

Did she call you?

base verb after did

He said me that he was tired.

He told me that he was tired.

tell + person; say + that

She suggested me to wait.

She suggested waiting.

suggest + -ing (or that + clause)

I look forward to meet you.

I look forward to meeting you.

'to' here is a preposition

I enjoy to read.

I enjoy reading.

enjoy + -ing

He made me to wait.

He made me wait.

make + person + base verb

I will get my car to repair.

I will get my car repaired.

have/get + object + participle

The house was builted in 1990.

The house was built in 1990.

past participle of build = built

My phone was stolen by me.

I lost my phone.

active is clearer for your own actions

The book what I read…

The book (that) I read…

no 'what' as a relative pronoun

My mother, that lives…

My mother, who lives…

'that' is not used after commas

Never I have seen such a mess.

Never have I seen such a mess.

inversion after negative openers

He mustn't be at home.

He can't be at home.

can't = deduction; mustn't = prohibition

Would you mind to open the window?

Would you mind opening the window?

mind + -ing

I am very interesting in history.

I am very interested in history.

-ed = feels; -ing = causes

Opening the window, the room was cold.

Opening the window, I felt the cold.

participle subject must match

He denied to break it.

He denied breaking it.

deny + -ing

Unless you don't hurry…

Unless you hurry…

'unless' already means 'if not'

APPENDIX 3 · ESSENTIAL SENTENCE PATTERNS FOR SPEAKING

Build answers from these skeletons until they are automatic

Function

Patterns

Experience

I have (never) … · One experience that changed me was …

Story

First … Then … After that … Suddenly … Finally …

Opinion

I believe that … because … · From my point of view …

Reason

This is mainly because … · The main reason is that …

Example

For instance … · A good example of this is …

Contrast

Although …, … · Despite + noun/-ing … · On the other hand …

Concession

It is true that …; nevertheless … · Admittedly …; even so …

Result

As a result … · This means that … · Consequently …

Hedged claim

It could be argued that … · … may well … · … tend(s) to …

Emphasis

It is … that … · What I mean is … · I do believe …

Advice

If I were you, I'd … · You might want to … · It might be worth …

Regret

I wish I had … · If only I had … · What I should have done was …

Preference

I'd rather … than … · I prefer … to … · If I had to choose, I'd …

Prediction

In the future, … will probably … · … is likely to …

Polite request

Would you mind …-ing? · Could I possibly …? · I was wondering if …

Reporting

He said (that) … · She pointed out that … · They warned me not to …

Description

…, who/which … · The person who … · …, which means that …

Comparison

… is far more … than … · The more …, the more … · … is by far the most …

Process

First, … is done; then … is … · Having been …, … · … is then …

Summary

To sum up … · All in all … · The point I want to make is …

Self-repair

What I mean is … · Let me rephrase that … · Or rather …

Ending

That's why … · This taught me that … · Looking ahead, I plan to …
